That is the correct reduction of the program you wrote.

Here are the steps as done by a lambda evaluator (using hvm-lang syntax)
```
(List ((Two Take) (T (T F))))
(((Two (Cons I)) F) ((Two Take) (T (T F))))
(((λf λx (f (f x)) (Cons I)) F) ((Two Take) (T (T F))))
((λx ((Cons I) ((Cons I) x)) F) ((Two Take) (T (T F))))
(((Cons I) ((Cons I) F)) ((Two Take) (T (T F))))
(((λx λy λz ((z x) y) I) ((Cons I) F)) ((Two Take) (T (T F))))
((λy λz ((z I) y) ((Cons I) F)) ((Two Take) (T (T F))))
(λz ((z I) ((Cons I) F)) ((Two Take) (T (T F))))
((((Two Take) (T (T F))) I) ((Cons I) F))
((((λf λx (f (f x)) Take) (T (T F))) I) ((Cons I) F))
(((λx (Take (Take x)) (T (T F))) I) ((Cons I) F))
(((Take (Take (T (T F)))) I) ((Cons I) F))
(((λcont λx λxs λz ((z x) (xs cont)) (Take (T (T F)))) I) ((Cons I) F))
((λx λxs λz ((z x) (xs (Take (T (T F))))) I) ((Cons I) F))
(λxs λz ((z I) (xs (Take (T (T F))))) ((Cons I) F))
λz ((z I) (((Cons I) F) (Take (T (T F)))))
λz ((z I) (((λx λy λz ((z x) y) I) F) (Take (T (T F)))))
λz ((z I) ((λy λz ((z I) y) F) (Take (T (T F)))))
λz ((z I) (λz ((z I) F) (Take (T (T F)))))
λz ((z I) (((Take (T (T F))) I) F))
λz ((z I) (((λcont λx λxs λz ((z x) (xs cont)) (T (T F))) I) F))
λz ((z I) ((λx λxs λz ((z x) (xs (T (T F)))) I) F))
λz ((z I) (λxs λz ((z I) (xs (T (T F)))) F))
λz ((z I) λz ((z I) (F (T (T F)))))
λz ((z I) λz ((z I) (λx λy y (T (T F)))))
λz ((z I) λz ((z I) λy y))
```

You are right. I forgot that my take function misbehaves if the number of elements taken is greater than or equal to the length of the given list.
I originally wrote it for taking elements from an infinite list, where this is never an issue.
Sorry for the false alarm!

I think this program loops forever because it's not possible to extract `L` into a supercombinator so it will expand infinitely.

If i define `L` like this it should work:
```haskell
L = λself λn (λz (z T (self (I n))))
Main = (T I (L L I))
```

The program should just return (T I (L L I)) = I.
It's an if True then I else L I so what L does should be irrelevant.

Btw, this is a trimmed down version of a prime number sieve where L is an infinite list of booleans, that gives the same error:

B0 = λx λy x
B1 = λx λy y
K = B0
Nil = B1
Cons = λx λy λz (z x y)
Cons0 = (Cons B0)
Two = λb λc (b (b c))
Three = λb λc (b (b (b c)))
Four = λb λc (b (b (b (b c))))
Y = λf ((λx (x x)) (λx (f (x x))))
S0    = λcont  λx λxs (Cons0  (xs cont))
Ssucc = λSn λc λx λxs (Cons x (xs (Sn c)))
Sieve = λSn (Cons B1 ((λSsn (Sieve Ssn (Y Ssn))) (Ssucc Sn)))
Primes = (Cons0 (Cons0 (Sieve S0)))
Take = λcont λx λxs λz (z x (xs cont))
Main = (Primes (Four Take (K (K Nil))))
You're right, this program returns the identity function. But since the runtime is eager, `(L I)` will not be ignored and the problem I commented will occur
How does one program necessary lazy constructs then, such as is if-then-else?

You can do it as long as your recursive functions are not directly being called in themselves (or similar more complicated recursive patterns).

For example, you can write an if function like this:
```
false = λx λy x
true = λx λy y
if = λx λthen λelse (x then else)
```
Then, if your function needs to take an argument, you pass it later, to keep the lazyness:
```
is_zero = λn match n {0: true; 1+*: false}
is_even = λn ((if (is_zero n) (λ* true) is_odd) (- n 1))
is_odd = λn ((if (is_zero n) (λ* false) is_even) (- n 1))
```
Notice how here we need an additional `λ` compared to what we might write for a lazy evaluator
```
is_even = λn (if (is_zero n) true (is_odd (- n 1)))
```
In general, as long as the recursive part is written as a combinator, it will work fine

K = λx λy x

Cons = λx λy λz (z x y)
Fib = λa λb (Cons a (λz (Fib b (+ a b))))
Main = (Fib 0 1 K)

I stuck an extra λ into Fib to allow eager evaluation.

`Function '+' cannot be applied to arguments (Lam, Num). Only (Num, Num) are valid.` or something like this? Dont know if its possible at all though, since this seems like a low level machine.

That will come when we write the type checker for hvml (very soon).

For the runtime underneath, an invalid interaction is like an invalid opcode in a VM. And it's even harder to know exactly what was the origin since data and instructions are the same thing, after a function is applied we lose all information about the source of that inet.

A license is the constitution of the community. If you use a
permissive license or a CLA, it's a signal that you may plan to make
the project proprietary and that community contributions are "free as
in labour" not "Free as in Freedom". There's nothing necessarily wrong
with that, but it's good to be clear and transparent with your
community so they can know what to expect. GPLv3 protects the
interests of your community, Apache v2 (ALv2) protects the interests
of your company (but it can back fire because others can fork and
leave you in the dust!). It's up to the project to decide, but a
decision is pretty important. It's more complicated than that, but
this project seems neat, so I'm happy to answer questions offline if
that would help them.

James

I also suggest keeping in mind Conway's game of life type workloads where data has to be constantly transferred between (MPI) processes (that don't share memory with each other). Local process has to send copies of (some of) its cells to other processes so that they can calculate next iteration of their cells, and they have to send copies of their cells to local process so that it can calculate next iteration of its cells, repeated N times.

Supporting explicit calls to MPI functions is important for these workloads because balancing computation and communication is a science unto itself (one library that helps with this is sandialabs.github.io/Zoltan/Zoltan_phil.html for example) so trying to do that automatically most likely wouldn't work.

Your fibonacci function creates a tree of addition operators of size ~2^n. It fails at large numbers because you run out of memory (maximum of 2^29 nodes at once) and it is slow because your implementation is exponentially slow.
Here's a sequential implementation that scales linearly
```
fib x =
  bend x a=1 b=1 {
     when (!= x 0): (fork (- x 1) b (+ a b))
     else: a
  }
```

I don't think this is trivial, because there is a fundamental difference between multicore shared-memory parallelism and distributed parallelism as allowed by MPI.

To begin with, I'm assuming you mean adding multiprocess capabilities to the HVM evaluator via an MPI implementation (and not just MPI bindings to bend-lang). I just took a look at this myself (so I apologize if I say anything non-factual), but it looks like parallel rewrites are performed without locks (using a fairly straightforward algorithm facilitated by atomic instructions). 

I am willing to bet a good sum of money that this is key to getting reasonable performance out of this in cases where the combinator graph is "highly interconnected" (high edge/vertex ratio, high average degree, a lot of cliques), as the cost of locking would be particularly severe here.

That being said, it would be good to have some kind of a (potentially implicit) API to partition the combinator graph into large enough sufficiently independent subgraphs (see "cheeger constant" and "conductance" for related formalisms) as a mechanism to control the overhead of locking. Then, it would be possible to distribute these partitions to different MPI nodes, allowing them to alter contested combinators through distributed locking and all other combinators as usual (through atomic intrinsics).

For example, we could define this "API" to be "functions with an underscore in front of them are assumed to be very computationally intensive." (Or at least, intensive enough for the overhead of distribution to be worth it). Then, something like this:

```
_sum_big(_matmul_big(A, B), _matmul_big(C, D))
```

..could be performed on two different nodes in parallel. Of course, I have not even visited the question of the overhead of moving data -- sometimes the computation will not be "complex," but it will not be worth it to do it in another node because of this cost (e.g., is `_matmul_big` costly because the matrices are big, or because it is an expensive algorithm?).

There are also other more specific yet just as important questions, like whether or not RDMA is present. All of this complicates things a lot, and probably requires theoretical groundwork before spending any time on an implementation.

@iljah 

I think that the whole point of Bend / the HVM is to automate parallelism. As such (and as you mentioned), there would be nothing special about adding MPI bindings -- there is already an issue for a FFI (see #350). 

I obviously think that FFI support will be an important component for Bend if it ever wants to make it to production, as the classic optimization for hot code will always be to write it in C and compile it with a SOTA compiler. I am not refuting the value of that. (Not to mention access to tried and tested libraries in the first place). 

For this reason, I think this conversation should be about getting MPI to be automatically used by the HVM in the process of  rewriting the interaction net, and not about adding MPI bindings. (I swear, if Bend gets complete MPI bindings before Rust, I will be an unhappy individual).

However, the "existing libraries" you quote (which would go into the HVM and analyze the combinator graph) are nowhere near performant enough to be used there. I'm not saying they're not well implemented, I'm saying that the algorithms they execute are way too costly to run every time there is a rewrite of an interaction combinator. I am not saying there is no fast enough algorithm to do this in the specific case of a combinator net -- but that is something that we would need a peer-reviewed paper on to build anything meaningful on top of.

This doesn't mean it's over though, in particular because this is a runtime we are talking about (so it is possible to keep statistics about it and make very good estimations). See below for more.

@maxboone 

Thanks Max. As I mentioned in my reply to @iljah, I agree -- it would be most utilitarian to first have a FFI. And right, something like this would be useful for other kinds of hardware offloading in general.

I think there is a lot of work to reference (in particular in the JVM's JIT compiler) when it comes to cost estimation. And yes, switching to C++ would probably be the most direct path for the HVM, since that is where this would happen (not the bend-lang compiler). 

Regardless of that, to reiterate -- I think the main attraction of this is automatically invoking different forms of hardware offloading when necessary. An FFI should come first (actually, I/O should come even before that), but implementing generic hardware offloading would be a killer feature. Imagine autoscaling the map-reduce example backed by a distributed MapReduce system, or having OpenMPI automatically distribute ML workloads across different nodes, and having all of these decisions being done automatically by the runtime (with a lot of hints from the developer, probably).

> Why won't every single monads work?

If you have a program like
```
def Z(x1, x2):
do Result:
  a <- X(x1)
  b <- Y(x2)
  c <- Z(a, b)
  ...
```
This is converted to ```(Result/bind (X x1) @a (Result/bind (Y x2) @b (Result/bind (Z a b) ...)```
Note that the call to `(Z a b)` is not a combinator and so cannot be converted to a lazy reference. This will cause Z to be expanded infinitely.
For this to actually work, we need to do some transformation on this term that will convert it into ```(...(Result/bind @a @b (Z a b) ...)```.
I haven't yet found a transformation that works on every possible monad, although I have some good directions to explore.


> Why not name it `return`?

Because `return` already returns. I don't know how to make it not clash with the existing syntax.

Some thoughts about this:
* Adding PGO to the Bend build looks very promissing, probably will be done at some point.
* Bend goes out of the way to have as few dependencies as possible, especially at its core. So I doubt link-time optimizations will improve too much.
* The Bend compiler is NOT optimized, almost at all. Our focus so far has been on correctness and simplicity. Before investigating compile optimizations, we'll have to profile and optimize the logic of Bend itself, which I imagine will bring much greater improvements.
* I'm much more interested in the performance this can bring to the runtime. We should try doing this to the C runtime. I imagine that for CUDA, PGO is not really a thing?

> Bend goes out of the way to have as few dependencies as possible, especially at its core. So I doubt link-time optimizations will improve too much.

Probably - at least it should improve the binary size. This optimization is already enabled (so I changed nothing for this in the build scripts).

> The Bend compiler is NOT optimized, almost at all. Our focus so far has been on correctness and simplicity. Before investigating compile optimizations, we'll have to profile and optimize the logic of Bend itself, which I imagine will bring much greater improvements.

Yep. However, even after performing manual optimizations with a higher probability PGO still will be useful. All modern "mature" compilers like Clang, Rustc, GCC, and many others still have large performance benefits from enabling PGO for them.

> I'm much more interested in the performance this can bring to the runtime. We should try doing this to the C runtime. I imagine that for CUDA, PGO is not really a thing?

It depends. If we talk about GPU code - yes, PGO is not a thing yet for it. If we talk about the CPU part - PGO should work as for regular non-CUDA code.

Conversion from HVM to Bend can have more than one possible interpretation.
The resulting net, in HVM syntax is `(((a a) *) (b b))`
`((λa a, *), λb b)` is one valid form of the result.
Another equally valid result would be `let * = (a λc c); λa λb b`, which is the one you're expecting.

Currently the heuristic for deciding if a node is a lambda or a tuple is very simplistic and will give some unexpected results.

You *can* use `_` or any other variable name as a wildcard in matches.
```
type MyMap:
  Full { val, ~lft, ~rgt }
  Empty { ~lft, ~rgt }
  Leaf

def foo(map):
  match map:
    case MyMap/Leaf:
      ...
    case m:
      ...
```
Here `case m` matches both the `Full` and the `Empty` cases.

However, I think you're misunderstanding what `match` does. It does not match on multiple possible types and we will not change it to do so.
With the way that we internally represent constructors and pattern matching it is impossible to do so. We could chage it to make that possible, but that would incentivize users to make really hard to understand programs, so we won't.

Yes, passing the wrong number of arguments will break your program.
Bend is untyped and fully curried, so we have no way of knowing if passing an extra argument is valid or not.

We could add a special check for `fork` to force you to pass exactly the expected number of arguments, but I'd rather wait for us to add a type checker instead of adding a lot of bandages to try to fix something that is fundamentally unfixable with our approach.

To run general programming in a massively parallel way by default. The advanced concepts (that are not really that complicated or advanced) that make it possible are not that important to users.
CUDA is really good for writing a very specific set of programs, but for everything else it becomes so complicated to write an efficient program that it must either be done by incredible specialists or it's just not done at all.

For those programs that CUDA is really good (like tensor operations), Bend is not at all a competitor. GPUs and CUDA are designed from the ground up to do those very specific things incredibly efficiently.

* `a | b` = log(a, b), log_b(a)
* `a ^ b` = pow(a, b), a^b

I'd like to propose two seemingly unconsidered alternatives, each of which would fix the expression-statement issue:

- A C-like ternary operator
  Imperative syntax: `condition ? is_true : is_false`
  Functional syntax: `(? condition is_true is_false)`
- An `ifelse` function.
  Imperative syntax: `ifelse(condition, is_true, is_false)`
  Functional syntax: `(ifelse condition is_true is_false)`

The C-like option would be less Python-like, but would still be familiar to most developers and would be more concise. On the other hand, the `ifelse` option would be more Python-like, but would run the risk of potentially breaking programs that have an `ifelse` in their namespace.

> What syntax to use for type variables.

Regarding generics, Kind2 does it with the diamond operator following the name of the function being defined. For example:
```
concat <T> (xs: (List T)) (ys: (List T)) : (List T) =
  match xs {
    ++: (cons xs.head (concat xs.tail ys))
    []: ys
  }
```
It's also similar to other existing languages, so I think it's nice.

With Hindley-Milner, it would be possible to automatically "float" any undefined names to type quantifiers, but I personally think being explicit is better.

Ok here's what I settled on.

First version has types only on functions. Possibly will need to add annotation expressions later to mix typed and untyped code.

For imp syntax
```
# <var1, ..., varn> for type vars
# args can be given a type with `: Type`
# Type constructors are like normal function applications
# Since types and values never cross, `object` can share its type name with the constructor name.
# Can declare type variables in a type expression with `forall a, b: ...` or `∀a, b:`
# Eg. `def const(val: u24) -> forall t: t -> u24:`. Not sure of the usefulness but seems like we should have the option.
# Arrow types are infix `ArgType -> RetType`.
# Tuple types are written like tuples `(a, b)`
# Superpositions are not in the type system.
# Affinity is not in the type system.
# `Any` type will typecheck with anything. Default type of unchecked things
# Other builtin types are `u24`, `f24`, `i24` and `None` (the type of `*` as a value, a unit type).
def foo <a, b> (x: Ctr(a), y: a -> b, z, w: Any) -> OtherCtr -> b:
  ...
# Can mark a function as having a trusted unchecked type with `unchecked def`.
# This is needed for functions with superposition, unscopeds, other non-lambda things.
unchecked def channel<a, b>() -> (a -> b, b -> a):
  return (lambda $a: $b, lambda $b: $a)
# Untyped arguments and returns are given type `Any`
def foo(a, b):
  ...
# same as
def foo(a: Any, b: Any) -> Any:
```

Fun syntax
```
# Functions can be preceeded by a type signature
foo <a> <b> (x: a) (y: b) : a -> b
foo x y = ...

# Signatures can have parens like pattern matching rules
(reverse <t> (xs: (List t)) (acc: (List t))) : (List t)
(reverse (Cons x xs) acc) = (reverse xs (Cons x acc))
(reverse  Nil        acc) = acc

# If only one non-pattern matching rule, we can write the equation and the signature together like in Kind
(reverse <t> (xs: (List t)) : (List t) = (reverse.go xs [])
# Type ctrs use parens around like function calls
# forall is written `forall var body` or `∀var body` like lambdas are. No patterns allowed.
# Arrow type is still infix
# Everything else same as above
fold <a> <b> (xs: (List a)) (cons: a -> b -> b) (nil: b) : b

# Unchecked functions start their signature with `unchecked`
unchecked channel <a> <b> : (a -> b, b -> a) = (@$a b, @$b a)
```

Hvm definitions are always unchecked, but accept a type
```
# Uses imp syntax
hvm to_u24 -> forall a: (a -> u24):
  ...
```

The needed builtin types to cover all the operations we have so far are
* `Any`, for untyped things
* `None`, for `*` (erasure)
* `u24`, `f24` and `i24`, the three types of native numbers
* `Number(t)` the polymorphic type that accepts any of the three numbers as parameter
* `Integer(t)` the polymorphic type that accepts `i24` and `u24` as parameter. Needed for bitwise operations.
* `Float(t)` the polymorphic type that accepts only `f24`. Not strictly needed at the moment, but will be if we ever add more native floating point numbers. For things like `sin`, `log`, etc.
* `(t1, ..., tn)` the type of tuples. Technically multiple types.

Skimming over the output, i notice two changes:

=============

Some differences seem to come from changes in either the linearization or eta-reduction. The new version generates some definitions smaller, probably by reordering some lambdas which allows them to be eta-reduced (basically generating a better linearization).

We can see this in the `swap` function
```hs
# old
swap = λa λb λc ((switch a {0: swap_c0; _: swap_c1}) c b)
swap_c0 = λa λb (b, a)
swap_c1 = λa λb (a, b)

# new
swap = λa switch a {0: swap_c0; _: swap_c1}
swap_c0 = λa λb (a, b)
swap_c1 = λa λb (b, a)
```
The same thing happens in `down`, `flow` and `warp`.

This being the source of the slowdown would be problematic because the new version is strictly smaller, with fewer rewrites. I don't think I can predict what exactly is the effect of ordering the arguments on performance, so it would be hard to generate always the fastest code.

================

In the old version, we lifted the calls to `sort` and `gen` in `main` to their own separate functions.
This lets `sum` start one iteration earlier than `sort` and both start earlier than `gen`.

We have to do this because otherwise in a lot of cases a program would just return a lazy reference without calling it.
For example, the three calls in main could be lifted together into their own definition and swapped by a reference. If we didn't inline the reference then the program would do nothing.

Something like this:
```
main = do_main
do_main = sum(20, sort(20, 0, gen(20, 0)))
```
Here it's quite stupid, but in a more general setting this was happening automatically a lot. It's not easy to decide when we need and when we don't need to to this, so it's always done.

This is quite easy to test, we just have to manually write the old one.

If this is the source of the slowdown, then we need to figure out a better heuristic for when to lift the functions in main that maximizes the speed of execution. Although in this case I don't think that's the problem since both `sum` and `sort` depend on the output generated by `gen` to do anything, so they should become somewhat synchronized automatically.

I was thinking that maybe we could have a stack of things we're expecting in the state of the parser.

Once we're 100% sure that we're expecting something more specific then we can push a new thing to the stack. Then if an error occurs we just look at the top one.

Something like:
* Start expecting a top-level definition
* Parse `def`, expect a function definition.
* Parsing the function name, expect a top-level name, then pop.
* Parsing `(`, expect `(`, etc.

But importantly, when we have an alternative and we didn't match any of the "guard" clauses that identify a specific alternative, we still expect the construct one level above.
So for example, if the parser didn't find `def`, `type` or `object`, it'll try to parse a fun-syntax function definition but still give an error of `expected top-level definition`.

This would be a generalization of the `labelled` logic that allows for nested labels.

Interestingly, you've had the opposite reaction from what most other users did, who've complained mostly about `bend` and almost never about `fold`.

`fold` replaces the recursive fields with their folds. If users had to `reduce` like you say, then there would be the option of not doing so, which would make it no longer a fold. This is the reason for it being implicit, and we want to encourage users to write programs as folds.

Not having it be implicit would make `fold` an inline generic multiple recursion on adts, and programs that mix parts of `fold` that do recurse and parts that don't would suddenly be much more confusing.

I agree that having it implicit is a bit confusing, even after you're familiarized with the syntax, because it means that accessing a field has different meaning depending on the surrounding context (match vs fold), but I don't know a better way.

Then, when we added folds with state, where the recursive fields are replaced with a fold function that receives the state, we just didn't introduce any new syntax at all and just used things the way they naturally expressed themselves.

And yes, the guide does need to be improved quite a bit, I'll be sure to pass this issue to the guys that are currently working on the documentation.

`get_initial_board` gets passed as the argument `board` and then cloned inside `get_possible_moves`.

This is one of the cases where the heuristic for finding the problematic cases is too strict. This function has some duplications inside it, but not in its normalized form.

The function desugars to `Map/set(Map/set(Map/set(Map/empty, 0, black), 1, white), 2, empty)`, and `Map/set` duplicates the key (0, 1 and 2 in this example). However, after normalizing, `get_initial_board` reduces to just an ADT value and not a function so the duplications are not a problem.

Unfortunately this check happens directly at runtime with no way of disabling it for your specific function. Ideally we'd have a type system that can assertain whether or not a value will have problematic duplications, but that's not planned for the immediate future.

For now, you can circumvent this issue by applying a dummy value to the function that forces its evaluation:
```python
def get_initial_board(dummy):
  return { 0: black, 1: white, 2: empty }

...

def main():
  board = get_initial_board(*)
```

It seems that the type checker is unifying the `Any` type of the `unreachable` too eagearly.

When checking a `match`, it infers the type of all match arms, unifies them all and then at the end unifies against the type annotation. Since `Any` forcefully casts everything into it, the incorrect type of the first arm (`Maybe(Maybe(T))`) is erased and replaced by `Any` which will type check without issues when unifiying against the `Maybe(T)` annotation.

A better checking algorithm would be to check each arm separately against the annotation, but that will require substantial changes to how the type checking algorithm is structured.

Bend core terms directly compile to HVM nodes.
Application -> CON node with --+ polarization.
Lambda -> CON node with ++- polarization.
Duplication -> DUP node with -++ polarization.
Superposition -> DUP node with +-- polarization
Pairs -> CON node with +-- polarization.
Pair elimination -> CON node with -++ polarization.
Erasure values (as in `λx *`) -> ERA node with + polarization.
Erased variables (as in `λ* x`) -> ERA node with + polarization.
Numbers -> NUM node (always + polarization).
Switches -> MAT node (--+) + CON node (+--) on port 1 that links to the if 0 and if >= 1 cases.
Numeric operations -> an OPR node (--+) plus a NUM that holds the kind of operation as per the HVM2 paper.
References to top level functions -> REF node (+).

Matches get compiled to the above core constructs according to the adt-encoding option.

The rest of the compilation process is (should be) described in the other documents. We have the following (relevant to this document) compiler passes:
- encode_adt : create functions for constructors
- desugar_open : convert `open` terms into `match` terms
- encode_builtins : convert sugars for builtin types (list, string, etc) into function calls.
- desugar_match_def : convert equational-style pattern matching functions into trees of match and switch terms.
- fix_match_terms : puts all match and switch terms into a normalized form.
- lift_local_defs : converts def terms into top-level functions.
- desugar_bend : converts bend terms into top-level functions.
- desugar_fold : converts fold terms into top-level functions.
- desugar_with_blocks : converts with terms and ask (<-) terms into monadic bind and unit (wrap).
- make_var_names_unique : Give a unique name to each variable in each function.
- desugar_use : resolve alias terms (use) by substituting their occurences by the aliased term (syntatic duplication).
- linearize_matches : linearize the variables in match and switch terms according to the linearize-matches option.
- linearize_match_with : linearize the variables specified in with clauses of match and switch if they haven't already been linearized by linearize_matches.
- type_check_book : runs the type checker (no elaboration, only inference/checking).
- encode_matches : transform match terms into their lambda-calculus forms specified by the adt-encoding option.
- linearize_vars : linearizes the occurences of variables by placing dups when variables are used more than once, erasing unused variables and inlining let terms whose variables only occur once.
- float_combinators : converts combinator terms into top-level functions according to the size heuristic described in the source code and probably in another document.
- prune : removes unused functions according to the prune option.
- merge_definitions : merge identical top level functions.
- expand_main : expands the term of the main function by dereferencing so that it includes some computation and isn't only lazy refs or data containing lazy refs.
- book_to_hvm : the lowering to hvm described in the compilation-and-readback file.
- eta : runs eta-reduction on the inet level, without reducing nodes with ERA or NUM at both ports (logically equivalent but for users it looks wrong).
- check_cycles : a heuristic check for mutually recursive cycles of function calls that would cause loops in the HVM.
- inline_hvm_book : inlines REFs to networks that are just nullary nodes.
- prune_hvm_book : another layer of pruning (new things can pop up after eta-reducing at the inet level).
- check_net_sizes : ensures that no generated definition will be too large to run on the cuda runtime.
- add_recursive_priority : marks some binary recursive calls with a flag at the inet level so that the gpu runtime can properly distribute work.

The documentation should also link to the HVM2 paper instead of the old hvm-64.

This is the intended rule, not a bug: the checker compares the call's arguments to the parameters from left to right; each must be passed unchanged until one is a strict subterm of its pattern, and the rest are free (the BendTT paper's Descent section states it, and tests/halt/threaded_state_before.bend pins your exact case). We cannot accept "any argument shrinks, the others arbitrary": that rule admits a cycling program (tests/halt/size_change_reject_000.bend), while the left-to-right law stays sound and still accepts Ackermann. Reproduced on current main (0b7e2b1, `VERSION = "2.0.5"`), compiling through the loader in `bend2/main.ts` and running the emitted JS under Node 20.20 and Bun 1.4.2. Same numbers as yours: `String.split` and `String.length` throw `RangeError` at 10k chars on Node and at 20k/100k on Bun.

Two things to add.

**1. `String.take` is not special, and it is not native.** In `base.bend` it has the exact same shape as `split`/`length` (`SCon{h, String.take(t, p)}`, non-tail), and the emitter has no intrinsic for it. It only looked fine because your test calls `String.take(s, 5n)`: recursion depth is `n`, not the string length. Calling it with `n` = string length overflows at the same sizes:

```
runtime: node v20.20.2
10000 String.take 5 ok 5
10000 String.take n ERR RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
100000 String.take n ERR RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
```

Same family at 100k chars on Node: `String.to_upper` and `String.to_list` throw as well. `String.reverse`, `String.drop`, `String.trim` are fine because their self-call is already in tail position (they go through `run_jump`). `String.append` is fine because `comp.ts` maps it to a native (`string_append: { JS: "($0 + $1)" }`), so there is precedent for the native route you suggest.

**2. Workaround that works today, no compiler change.** Write the two functions accumulator-style so the self-call is in tail position; the JS backend then emits `run_jump` and the trampoline keeps the stack flat. Mutual recursion is not allowed and `match` cannot scrutinize a computed value, so the per-char decision goes into a non-recursive step helper that returns the new state as a tuple:

```bend
def Str.length.go(s: String, acc: Nat) -> Nat:
  match s:
    case SNil{}:
      acc
    case SCon{h, t}:
      Str.length.go(t, 1n+acc)

def Str.length(s: String) -> Nat:
  Str.length.go(s, 0n)

# state = (current piece, reversed; pieces so far, reversed)
def Str.split.step(h: Char, st: String & List<&2, String>, cut: Bool) -> String & List<&2, String>:
  (cur, acc) = st
  match cut:
    case True{}:
      (SNil{}, String.reverse(cur) <> acc)
    case False{}:
      (SCon{h, cur}, acc)

def Str.split.fin(st: String & List<&2, String>) -> List<&2, String>:
  (cur, acc) = st
  List.reverse(&2, String, String.reverse(cur) <> acc)

def Str.split.go(s: String, +sep: Char, st: String & List<&2, String>) -> List<&2, String>:
  match s:
    case SNil{}:
      Str.split.fin(st)
    case SCon{+h, t}:
      Str.split.go(t, sep, Str.split.step(h, st, Char.is_eq(h, sep)))

def Str.split(s: String, +sep: Char) -> List<&2, String>:
  Str.split.go(s, sep, (SNil{}, Nil{}))
```

Checks clean. Output matches `String.split` from Base on the edge cases I tried (empty string, leading/trailing/adjacent separators, astral chars), and it handles your 11 MB case:

```
runtime: node v20.20.2
same ""            [""]
same ","           ["",""]
same ",a,,b,"      ["","a","","b",""]
same "😀,x😀y,,"    ["😀","x😀y","",""]
10000    Str.split (loop) ok 101     5ms     String.split(Base) ERR RangeError
100000   Str.split (loop) ok 1001    14ms    String.split(Base) ERR RangeError
1000000  Str.split (loop) ok 10001   133ms
11000000 Str.split (loop) ok 110001  1593ms
11000000 Str.length(loop) ok 11000000n 239ms
```

Emitted JS for the loop version, for comparison with the one in your report:

```js
function $Str$split$go$(s_0, sep_0, st_0) {
  if (s_0 === "") {
    return run_jump($Str$split$fin$, [st_0]);
  } else {
    const h_0 = (s_0.codePointAt(0) > 0xFFFF ? s_0.slice(0, 2) : s_0[0]);
    const t_0 = (s_0.codePointAt(0) > 0xFFFF ? s_0.slice(2) : s_0.slice(1));
    const h_1 = h_0;
    return run_jump($Str$split$go$, [t_0, sep_0, run_loop($Str$split$step$(h_1, st_0, run_loop($Char$is_eq$(h_1, sep_0))))]);
  }
}
```

One scoping note, so this is not read as more novel than it is.

`tests/show/string_escape.bend` already records part of point 2 as a known gap:

> A surrogate or a code past U+10FFFF is not pinned here: the JS lane holds a
> Char as a JS string and refuses those at char_new.

So "the JS lane refuses a surrogate at `char_new`" is understood, and a source
literal like `"\u{d800}"` hitting it is the same known gap (the parser takes it,
the C lane runs it, the JS lane dies) — treat that part as context, not a new find.

What I believe is new here is the decode seam rather than `char_new`:

- `io_str` and `TextDecoder` disagree on **all** invalid input, not just the
  non-scalar cases: `80` → `Chr{128}` vs `Chr{65533}`, `ff` → `Chr{255}`,
  `e6 97` → two chars vs one. These are plain mojibake, and no lane errors.
- `io_str` **accepts overlong encodings**: `c0 80` → `Chr{0}`.
- `String.length` of the same bytes differs (16 vs 21), so control flow and not
  just rendering diverges.
- On the way back out, `io_utf8` re-emits `ed a0 80` and `f7 bf bf bf` verbatim,
  so the C lane writes bytes that are not valid UTF-8 — which is the direction
  `tests/io/text_utf8.bend` and `print_utf8_law.bend` do pin.
- It reaches `TCP.recv`, `UDP.recv_from`, `UDP.poll` and `IO.get_env`, not just
  `File.read`, so it is on the untrusted-input paths.

A distinct resource-exhaustion regime on bend 2.0.5 (`main` @ e6676b0, Linux x86_64, bun 1.4.2): a sufficiently large *legal* literal never reaches a clean error at all.

```bend
import Base

def main() -> Nat:
  281474976710655n
```

`bend main.bend` produced no output for 90+ seconds at 99% CPU before being killed. (2^48−1 is the documented *runtime* immediate cap; the parser accepts literals up to `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`, so this literal is in-bounds as far as the parser is concerned.)

Unlike the moderate-literal case in this issue (validation stack overflow after parsing), the cost here appears to be the unary *expansion* itself — roughly one constructor node per successor, i.e. on the order of 10^14 nodes for this literal — though I did not instrument phases; the practical observation is "no diagnostic, unbounded work," and the threshold for overflow-vs-never-finishing varies with the host stack.

A hard, documented literal-size limit with a clean message (the U32 literal path already reports cleanly: `expected : a u32 literal up to 4294967295`) would turn both regimes into portable, legible errors.

Reproduced on 2.0.5 at commit `0b7e2b1`. Two things, both from the same session.

**1. The gate checks the laws the invoked file imports.** On
`demos/app_win_is_bug_2d`, whose `LAWS.bend` states two unproven laws
(`you_cant_win`, `never_on_flag`):

    All terms check.

    Error: 2 TODOs found.

The README tells agents to run `bend PROOF.bend` before committing, and
`PROOF.bend` is a file the agent writes. Whether that is a defect or the intended
contract is your call -- I am reporting the behaviour, not judging the design.

**2. The `@unsafe` disclosure is on the no-main path only.** `cli_report` is called
only from `book_run`'s no-main branch, and `cli_emit` never reports at all, so:

    bend PROOF.bend      -> "6 terms annotated as unsafe." + the paradox warning
    bend main.bend       -> the program's output, nothing else
    bend main.bend -o x  -> no output at all

I ran every demo proof: 4 of the 15 that ship one use `@unsafe`, including
`pure_hvm5_mini` with 6 unsafe terms. Each printed the banner only because it happens
to have no `main`. Under `bend main.bend` or any `-o`, the disclosure vanishes while
the unsafe def stays in the import graph.

Suggested, and both cheap: a non-zero exit while any `@unsafe` def is in the import
graph, and a way to require laws outside the agent-editable files -- either
`bend PROOF.bend --laws LAWS.bend`, or a refusal when a `LAWS.bend` beside it is not

The recursion is not specific to Base's string primitives. A hand-written
recursion using no Base string functions at all fails identically, so
rewriting `String.length` / `String.split` accumulator-style would hide this
rather than fix it:

```python
import Base

def mk(n: Nat, acc: String) -> String:
  match n:
    case 0n:
      acc
    case 1n+p:
      mk(p, SCon{'a', acc})

def len(s: String) -> Nat:
  match s:
    case SNil{}:
      0n
    case SCon{h, t}:
      1n+len(t)

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    IO.print(Nat.show(len(mk(U32.to_nat(30000), SNil{}))))
```

`bend m.bend` → `bend: memory fault (machine stack overflow?)`
`bend m.bend -o m && ./m` → `30000`

Cause is in the emitter. `js_call` (comp.ts:2931-2932) emits a non-tail call
as a nested host call:

```ts
: tail ? "run_jump(" + js_sat(k) + ", [" + exprs.join(", ") + "])"
: "run_loop(" + call + ")";
```

so only tail calls are trampolined and the host stack grows one frame per
level. Patching the emitted JS's `catch` in `io_run` to print the original
error gives `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` with a stack of
nothing but the recursive def. The C lane splits the same def at the cut,
mints a continuation segment (`FID_..._K8`) and pushes the frame on `STK`;
the JS lane has no equivalent.

Two things that may be useful for triage:

- The threshold is in frames, not bytes: 26552 ok / 26581 fails here, while a
  *tail*-recursive traversal of a 3,000,000-character string is fine. Total
  allocation is not the issue.
- `BUN_JSC_maxPerThreadStackUsage` raises the ceiling but saturates around
  42k frames for every value tried (8 MB: 42023 ok / 42080 fail; 32 MB — the
  value gates/test.ts sets: 41367 / 43261; 1 GB: 41367 / 45156). 300000 still
  fails. So it is not a mitigation, which matters given the gates rely on it.

Found using Claude.

Not a compiler hang: every stage finishes in under 0.3 s (check + C emit 0.065 s, clang 0.24 s). The program itself is the cost. `nfib(1n+p) = nfib(p) + nfib(p) + 1` calls `nfib(p)` twice, so it makes 2^(n+1) - 1 calls: 2.2e12 for n = 40. Bend does no common-subexpression elimination (`+n` only allows the copy), so both calls run. Measured on an M4 Max: n = 30 native in 1.67 s (1.3e9 calls/s), so n = 40 is about 28 minutes natively and hours on the JS lane. The usual nfib is `nfib(n-1) + nfib(n-2) + 1` (3e8 calls for n = 40). Closing.

Confirmed, and your diagnosis is exact: `+z` on a field is a rebinding let around the row body; once a later row's nested pattern refines that column, the let's value becomes a constructor, and a let must infer its value. We looked for a small fix and found none that does not either reach into the match flattener or add a type slot to lets or pattern binders (about 20-30 lines). Workaround: bind the field plainly in the pattern and rebind after the match (`+z2 = z` as the first line of the body), or keep the nested-pattern row above the `+` row.

Fixed on main (929157bc), ships in 2.0.8.

Cause: `+z` on a matched field was not a mark on the binder. The parser bound a fresh `z` and inserted a hidden let `+z' = z` after the match. When a later row split the same column, the flattener replaced that let's value with the reconstructed constructor, whose type the checker cannot infer: hence "cannot infer" on a program that is fine.

Fix: the `+` mark now lives on the pattern binder and travels to the lambda the flattener emits; the checker grants Many at a `+` binder whose type is Data. The hidden-let path is deleted. One visible change: a `+` on a field applies to that field's column in every row of the match, not only its own row.

Not a bug: your numbers fit the lane cube exactly. A bang runs 16384 lanes (128 x 128), so 4^7 leaves is the target: at 512^2 with 4x4 tiles, 7 levels = the cube (6 ms); 6 levels = a quarter (14 ms); 8-9 levels cost an extra kernel iteration each. At 128^2, 4 levels keep 256 lanes of 16384 busy (234 ms), 5 keep 1024 (87 ms), 6 keep 4096 (28 ms). The CPU pool is flat because 10 workers are fed by any of those leaf counts, so it cannot tune this. `bend guide shaders` (2.0.10) states the model, and 2.0.13 adds the rule of thumb you asked for: aim for 4^7 leaves per bang and sweep one level either side on the device.

I'm making a proper issue because I argue, as I did there, that this currently makes proof engineering for greenfield projects in Bend unworkable: every theorem about an abstraction must be re-proved wherever it is used on a new instance. 

This means that the proof count grows as theorems times instances rather than theorems plus instances. Each copy is checked, so the problem is not trust in any one proof, it is that every change to a law or a statement has to be redone in every copy, and nothing checks that the copies still state the same theorem.  At scale, you cannot do this with reasonable confidence that the semantics you want are what you have proved. Yes - not being able to reuse an hypothesis is part of the (current) language, by design, and the expressivity consequences of that are not fully stablished yet. For example, are there theorems we can't prove? Probably not. A simple workaround is to lift hypothesis out and "defunctionalize" your theorems, but that might lead to code size explosion. So, are there theorems that we can't prove *succinctly*? Probably.

That said, this is just an early limitation, and it will be addressed soon™, as noted in the paper. We have plenty of ways to do so, and the only reason we didn't is that no option is a clear winner and I want to make sure I make the best choice here.

For example, one way to introduce closure contraction is to extend it with Elementary Affine Logic style sharing. This would allow us to keep Type:Type, have contractible lambdas, and, as a bonus, compiling to HVM would be sound. This seems like a good direction to me, because it connects all the things I've worked on, and it gives Bend all the features of HVM (lazy optimal evaluation for higher order computations).

The problem of EAL is that I'm not sure whether that'd be ergonomic and practical. For one, we'd probably(?) need inference, which Bend currently avoids, because introducing explicit boxes in the middle of Pythonish syntax would be cumbersome. This requires research. If I decide this direction isn't right, we'll probably end up doing something more conventional, as in Idris 2, for example.

So, meanwhile, what should a user do?

1. For lower-order hypothesis: nothing (it works).

2. For higher-order: use templates (`~`). Covers most cases.

3. Otherwise: just use `unsafe`. Bend will admit lambda contraction today, but you'll get some warnings as it will disable the termination checker. Then, wait for a future update where Bend validates lambda contraction. As long as you're not doing something really silly, your proofs will still work, and the warnings will be gone. Also, consider posting them on BendHub, so we can actually test on it!

In short, the reason we choose to start with a fully affine core is merely so we stay flexible to pick the best possible way to add higher-order contraction, and we don't have that answer yet. But it is intended and will land whenever the underlying theory allows.

We cannot take this one, for a reason that is not obvious from the report it fixes.

**The premise does not hold.** `nextEventMatchingMask:untilDate:distantPast` *does* run the run loop. A probe with a run-loop observer, a version-0 source, a due timer and a main-queue block sees all of them serviced by that call, in 30-43 µs, with 8 observer callbacks — the same as passing `[NSDate date]`. GLFW's `_glfwPollEventsCocoa` and SDL's `Cocoa_PumpEvents` poll exactly this way. So the pump is not starving the window server.

**The deadline sits on the frame's critical path.** `window_show` pumps before `[layer nextDrawable]`, so with your change an empty queue blocks the frame for up to 2 ms before the drawable is taken. Measured on a 120 Hz display, means over 120-frame windows:

| | main | this PR | branch `pump` |
|---|---|---|---|
| plain window: frame gap | 8.40-8.96 ms | 8.33-9.10 ms | 8.33-8.48 ms |
| plain window: run-loop residency | 0.1-0.4% | 24.6-28.5% | 96.6-99.4% |
| `demos/app_slash_boss_3d`: frame gap | 8.32-8.40 ms | **12.4-14.0 ms** | 8.33-8.40 ms |

On a solid-colour window the 2 ms hides inside the vsync slack. On a real app it overruns the 8.33 ms period, so each frame takes about one and a half of them: 120 FPS becomes 72-80.

**What your report gets right is the fault underneath.** The main thread does sit outside the run loop for ~95% of an idle frame — blocked in `nextDrawable`, not in the pump. Branch `pump` (commit 59fcc766) fixes that at no frame cost: the Metal sequence moves to a `QOS_CLASS_USER_INTERACTIVE` helper thread and the main thread waits *inside* the run loop, woken by `CFRunLoopStop` when the frame is presented. Idle run-loop residency goes from 1% to 97-99% with the frame gap unchanged.

2.0.17 is out, and it takes your direction 1, with one part you did not ask for.

**What shipped.**

A `~` template's body is checked once, at its definition, against opaque constants: each leading `~` binder becomes a bodiless def of its domain, and the body must hold for every closed instance. A template is a theorem now, not a macro that is only checked where it is used. All 22 templates in Base passed unchanged; no rewrite was needed.

A `law` accepts `for ~k: T` while the `~` clauses lead. That is the move you said was unavailable: a law hypothesis that a proof may use as often as it needs.

An instance is no longer a re-reading of the template's text. `F(~a, ..)` elaborates to `F~n`, which **is** `F`'s body at `a`, minted and checked by the checker at the call. That closes a hole we found while doing this: the old parser re-parsed the template's source at each call site, so a module def that shadowed a Base name could make the checker and the compiled binary mean different things by one call. On 2.0.16 a lemma about such a call could be proved while the C binary computed something else; both now agree by construction. Because of this, a template instance no longer counts as unsafe: the 2.0.16 note your report quoted is gone.

The verdict changed with it. It no longer counts `@unsafe` marks; it names the defs that rely on unsafe, following calls and types (and constructor field types) to their closure:

```
All terms check, but 3 defs rely on unsafe:
- loop
- T
- main
```

Importing a module that holds an `@unsafe` def no longer marks a file that never calls it. It is not the quarantine you described — reliance is reported, not refused — but the report is now a fact about your development rather than a count of annotations in it.

**What did not change.** Packaging a law's hypotheses in a `Type`-kinded record still gives `expected : Data, observed : Type` outside `@unsafe`. Induction on an erased binder is still refused, and an erased proof field still lives in the dead fragment where Curry's paradox inhabits `{0n == 1n : Nat}`. Your failures 2 and 5 stand.

**Your question 2** — whether an opt-in graded proof fragment fits Bend's goals, or conflicts with the single universe and the one-pass checker — is Victor's to answer, and he will answer it himself. This reply does not speak for him on it.

`emit_fold` is a compile-time partial evaluator, and its fuel counted **unfolds**, not size: 64 unfolds per segment. A literal `Nat` bound makes every `match fuel` decidable, so a 60-step loop fits inside 64 unfolds and the whole loop lands in its caller. That is why `U32.to_nat(60)` changed everything: at 70 the fold aborts and the loop stays a loop.

The fuel is now the size of what an unfold adds (`FOLD_FUEL = 8192` term nodes). A wide body and a narrow one no longer cost the same. Measured on your own `gfx/05_craft.bend`: with a literal bound it emitted 22,049 lines and 950 kept terms; it now emits 9,115 lines and 6 kept terms, identical to the runtime-fuel version. Thank you for the writeup, and no.

Bend does no inference and no proof search, by design. It is a proof checker: you write the proof, and it tells you whether the proof is right. That is the whole job, and keeping it that small is what makes the kernel something a person can read and trust.

Automation belongs in a separate layer. A tool that talks to Why3, or to an SMT solver, and emits Bend proof terms is a perfectly good tool, and nothing stops anyone from building it against the language as it is. It should not live inside the checker, because then the checker's trust depends on it.

Closing as wontfix on the separation of concerns, not on the value of the idea.

`tri(10n)` makes 3^10 calls. The interpreter is a reference evaluator: it builds the term graph as it reduces, so its memory grows with the number of steps taken, not with the size of the answer. Nothing is leaking. On an M4 Max your file takes 4.7 s and 1.5 GB there, so it is not specific to Android or to Termux either.

If you meet a program where the interpreter's cost is NOT proportional to the steps it takes, that is a bug and we want to hear about it.

Three of your five points are already gone, and they went before this issue was filed. You measured 2.0.16; here is 2.0.18/2.0.19.

**Point 3, `for ~op` in a `law` is a parse error.** It parses now. Your own theorem is in our test suite as `tests/proof/reassoc4.bend`, stated over an abstract `op` with an abstract associativity law, and its proof applies the hypothesis twice:

```python
law reassoc4:
  for ~op: Nat -> Nat -> Nat
  for ~assoc: @x: Nat -> @y: Nat -> @z: Nat -> {op(op(x, y), z) == op(x, op(y, z)) : Nat}
  for +a: Nat
  for +b: Nat
  for +c: Nat
  for +d: Nat
  {op(op(op(a, b), c), d) == op(a, op(b, op(c, d))) : Nat}

def reassoc4(op, assoc, a, b, c, d):
  %assoc(a, b, op(c, d)) : {op(op(op(a, b), c), d) == _ : Nat}
  %Equal.sym(Nat, op(op(op(a, b), c), d), op(op(a, b), op(c, d)), assoc(op(a, b), c, d)) : {_ == op(op(a, b), op(c, d)) : Nat}
  {==}
```

`All terms check.` The `~` parameters are checked once with `assoc` an opaque constant, and a reference costs no usage, so the proof may use it as often as it needs. Each instance rides that one proof.

**Point 4, a template body is not checked until it is instantiated.** Fixed in 2.0.17. A `~` template is now an ordinary definition, and an instance is that definition applied to its `~` arguments; the body is checked generically. Your example, the one you say "checks although its proof cannot be right", is refused:

```
Error:
- expected : reassoc4~op(reassoc4~op(reassoc4~op(a, b), c), d)
- observed : reassoc4~op(a, reassoc4~op(b, reassoc4~op(c, d)))
```

**Point 4 again, every template instance counts as unsafe.** That was true in 2.0.16 and is not true now. The verdict counts `@unsafe` definitions and foreign definitions; a template counts as nothing. A file of templates prints `All terms check.`

**What is left is one thing, and you named it correctly.** A law about an abstract operation is a function-typed hypothesis, no function type is `Data`, so it cannot be marked `+`, and its second live use is refused. That is contraction of a non-`Data` value in live code. It is not about erased positions: a variable used twice in a type, in a law statement, in an `@`-quantified type, in a rewrite motive, or in an erased `-` argument or field is already unrestricted today, with no `+` anywhere. Every refusal in your report is a live use: your `assoc` is rewrite evidence, and your `s` is passed to `Semigroup.fold`'s own recursive call and to `Semigroup.op(s)`.

So the honest state is: for a structure known at compile time, `~` gives you the Mathlib move now, with the proof written once. For a structure chosen at run time, you need contraction, and that is a language decision Victor has written about publicly rather than something I can answer here. Your point 5, induction on an erased argument, is a separate wall and is not contraction.

My above comment about `unsafe` and "quarantine" was effectively that `unsafe` bearing modules (previously, every module in a library that used one) could allow theorem instances to be cheated by anyone that wanted to do so. The core issue as noted above remains: we still need to use explicit `unsafe` in a good number of instances because these are function-typed thoerems:

```python
# These are instance constructions: a record law field is a lambda, so its binders are run-time
# variables. `+` is not honored on a lambda binder, which is why each proof is
# lifted to a top-level def (Agda writes those as local where-definitions),
# and a `~` template cannot be instantiated at a variable, which is why these
# stay contracted instead of becoming certified templates.

# id: the identity functor. Its law fields delegate to top-level defs, since
# + is not honored on lambda binders.
@unsafe def identity.id_law(+C: Core.Category, +a: Core.Obj(C)) -> Core.HomEq(C)(a, a, Core.identity(C)(a), Core.identity(C)(a)):
  Core.refl(C)(a, a, Core.identity(C)(a))
```

The question was whether the interpreter should manage the memory being used, or if the expected behavior is for the compiler process to crash when it runs out of memory.

Update: a second pass cut most of the copy and start-up cost. The lane now beats 16 CPU threads on 10 of the 16 `bench/runtime/` programs (7 before), and every remaining loss is device time, not overhead. The patch is now 731 lines (`comp.ts` +546 −13, `main.ts` +9 −3).

**The heap is lazy now.** Before, each `!` copied the whole heap under the bump up and back down; tree-radix moved 3.7 GB over three turns. Now, after a device turn, the heap's 2 MB chunks are made inaccessible with `mprotect` and nothing is downloaded. The first host touch of a chunk faults and downloads that chunk alone; a chunk the host writes is marked dirty, and the next `!` uploads only dirty chunks. The result of a `!` is usually a few words, so tree-radix now moves 17 MB. The fault handler is chained in front of the stack-guard handler in `pool_stack`. Tracking by the bump alone is unsound: `heap_free` and `heap_alloc` rewrite freed slots in place under the old bump.

**Start-up.** My port zeroed 143 MB of a fresh `mmap` that was already zero: 0.10 s of a 0.25 s floor. Removed. The floor is now about 0.15 s, nearly all inside ROCm.

Wall seconds, medians of 3 runs, same protocol as above, all checksums correct:

| bench | 16 threads | HIP before | HIP now | device passes |
| - | - | - | - | - |
| gameoflife | 1.36 | 0.27 | **0.16** | 0.02 |
| mandelbrot | 0.68 | 0.28 | **0.16** | 0.01 |
| raytrace | 0.90 | 0.34 | **0.23** | 0.09 |
| merkle | 0.64 | 0.40 | **0.18** | 0.01 |
| kmeans | 0.95 | 0.45 | **0.27** | 0.13 |
| nbody | 0.65 | 0.26 | **0.19** | 0.01 |
| tree-radix | 0.83 | 1.37 | **0.49** | 0.27 |
| tree-matmul | 0.56 | 0.80 | **0.40** | 0.22 |
| tree-bitonic | 2.26 | 1.86 | **1.73** | 1.55 |
| bfs | 0.47 | 0.63 | **0.43** | 0.25 |
| symreg | 0.64 | 0.90 | 0.74 | 0.60 |
| hashmap | 0.48 | 1.14 | 0.59 | 0.41 |
| queens | 1.19 | 1.62 | 1.49 | 1.34 |
| terrain | 0.49 | 0.97 | 0.67 | 0.49 |
| editdist | 0.36 | 1.06 | 0.80 | 0.63 |
| lexer | 0.49 | 1.25 | 1.16 | 0.97 |

**The stock sizes understate uniform work.** They are 1 s programs, so the 0.15 s floor dominates. At 16 times the input, wall time against 16 threads: gameoflife 32x faster, nbody 21x, mandelbrot 14x, raytrace 10x, kmeans 8x. Device time scales linearly. queens and tree-bitonic stay near 1x at any size.

**The slow programs are two different problems.** I counted dispatches per lane in the work kernel. queens, symreg and editdist are imbalanced: in queens the mean lane does 9% of the longest lane's work, and in symreg one lane runs 3.8 times longer than all the others. lexer and tree-bitonic are balanced to 99%, so their cost is per dispatch and re-balancing cannot help. I tried in-kernel stealing from neighbouring rings: no gain, because after growth every lane holds exactly one task and there is nothing queued to steal. Growing for extra rounds to make smaller tasks made queens slower (1.5 s to 3.7 s).

**Checks on the final code.** The 11 runnable `!` tests are byte-identical to the CPU lane in both memory modes. My local copy of the gate gives 1299 / 1302, the same three failures as before. Two multi-turn tests where the host frees, rebuilds and extends device-built trees between `!` calls match a Python model. For concurrent faults I ran two tests 150 times each with 16 host threads folding a device-built tree: 300 of 300 correct, with about 41,000 faults waiting on the handler's lock and 32,000 finding their chunk already served by another thread.

**New weak point.** The handler calls `hipMemcpy` from SIGSEGV. The fault can only come from Bend's own evaluation code, never from inside ROCm, but POSIX does not promise it. A helper thread doing the download would be the clean form. The corpus is also a `memfd` now, so no transparent huge pages; I see no loss on these benchmarks.

One thing I noticed while testing, in unpatched behaviour: once the host pool has forked, a later `!` in the same program runs on the CPU, not the device. With a sequential host phase between them, both `!` calls reach the device.

PREFIX="${PREFIX:-/data/data/com.termux/files/usr}"

die() {

    exit 1
}

warn() {
    printf 'bend-termux: WARNING: %s\n' "$*" >&2
}

need() {
    command -v "$1" >/dev/null 2>&1 ||
        die "required command not found: $1"
}

need bun
need curl
need tar
need sed
need mktemp
need sha256sum
need cmp

case "$(uname -m)" in
    aarch64|arm64)
        ;;
    *)
        die "this updater is for Termux ARM64 only; detected: $(uname -m)"
        ;;
esac

# All validation runs are deliberately offline and must not create
# ~/.bend/check.json or contact bend-lang.com.
export BEND_NO_TELEMETRY=1

printf 'Reading official Bend release metadata...\n'

if ! INSTALLER="$(
    curl -fsSL \
        --retry 3 \
        --retry-delay 1 \
        --retry-connrefused \
        "$INSTALLER_URL"
)"; then
    die "failed to download official Bend installer metadata"
fi

# sed returns success even when there is no match, so these checks remain
# reachable under "set -euo pipefail".
VER="$(
    printf '%s\n' "$INSTALLER" |
        sed -n 's/^VER="\([^"]*\)".*$/\1/p' |
        sed -n '1p'
)"

SHA_LINUX_ARM64="$(
    printf '%s\n' "$INSTALLER" |
        sed -n 's/^SHA_LINUX_ARM64="\([^"]*\)".*$/\1/p' |
        sed -n '1p'
)"

[ -n "$VER" ] ||
    die "could not extract VER from official install.sh"

[ -n "$SHA_LINUX_ARM64" ] ||
    die "could not extract SHA_LINUX_ARM64 from official install.sh"

case "$VER" in
    ''|*[!0-9.]*)
        die "unexpected Bend version: $VER"
        ;;
esac

[ "${#SHA_LINUX_ARM64}" -eq 64 ] ||
    die "invalid SHA256 length from official installer"

SRC_URL="https://github.com/${REPO}/archive/refs/tags/v${VER}.tar.gz"
REL_URL="https://github.com/${REPO}/releases/download/v${VER}/bend-${VER}-linux-arm64.tar.gz"

TMP_BASE="${TMPDIR:-$PREFIX/tmp}"
mkdir -p "$TMP_BASE"

if ! TMP="$(mktemp -d "$TMP_BASE/bend-termux.XXXXXX")"; then
    die "failed to create temporary directory"
fi

SRC_ROOT="$TMP/src"
STAGE="$TMP/stage"
BACKUP="$TMP/backup"
SMOKE_BEND="$TMP/smoke.bend"
SMOKE_OUT="$TMP/smoke.out"

mkdir -p "$SRC_ROOT" "$STAGE" "$BACKUP"

ROLLBACK=0
HAD_BIN=0
HAD_BEND2=0
HAD_GUIDE=0
HAD_BIN_DIR=0

cleanup() {
    rc=$?

    if [ "$ROLLBACK" -eq 1 ]; then
        set +e

        rm -rf "$BEND_HOME/bend2"
        rm -rf "$BEND_HOME/guide"
        rm -f "$BEND_HOME/bin/bend"

        if [ "$HAD_BEND2" -eq 1 ] &&
           { [ -e "$BACKUP/bend2" ] || [ -L "$BACKUP/bend2" ]; }; then
            mv "$BACKUP/bend2" "$BEND_HOME/bend2"
        fi

        if [ "$HAD_GUIDE" -eq 1 ] &&
           { [ -e "$BACKUP/guide" ] || [ -L "$BACKUP/guide" ]; }; then
            mv "$BACKUP/guide" "$BEND_HOME/guide"
        fi

        if [ "$HAD_BIN" -eq 1 ] &&
           { [ -e "$BACKUP/bin/bend" ] || [ -L "$BACKUP/bin/bend" ]; }; then
            mkdir -p "$BEND_HOME/bin"
            mv "$BACKUP/bin/bend" "$BEND_HOME/bin/bend"
        fi

        if [ "$HAD_BIN_DIR" -eq 0 ]; then
            rmdir "$BEND_HOME/bin" 2>/dev/null || true
        fi

        printf 'bend-termux: previous Bend installation restored.\n' >&2
    fi

    rm -rf "$TMP"

Fixed in 2.0.21 (`bend update`).

The cause was where you placed it. `def_inst` mints an instance as a bodiless placeholder while its body is checked. When `bounce~0`'s body reached `loop(~Key{}, u)`, the key already named `loop~0`, and the placeholder came back unchecked: the "filled definition" guard had looked at the template `loop`, which has a body, and the self-call guard compares against the current lhs, which was `bounce~0`.

Now a reuse of an instance whose body is still being checked, from any other lhs, is refused as a self-call that does not decrease: it is a call back into an instance on the check stack, and no column of the current lhs can show it shrinking. Your two-node and three-node files both stop at the `loop` inside `~loop(~k)`:

```
- expected : a decreasing self-call (arguments are read left to right: each passed unchanged until one shrinks)
- observed : loop
```

An instance that calls itself directly with a shrinking argument still checks. Instances are minted depth first, so with re-entry refused the live call graph of instances is a tree plus descending self-loops, the same shape plain defs already have (a forward reference is undefined, so mutual recursion between defs is refused too). Your two-node file is pinned as `tests/check/template_inst_cycle.bend`.

The imported file's namespace makes `M.x` resolve to the real book key `cast~T.x`. Generic checking of the template `cast` creates the opaque parameter name `cast~T.x` from `k + "~" + h.k`, shadowing that imported definition in `gen.tlds`. The body therefore checks as a value of `Data`. Outside the temporary generic book, the same reference is the real `x : Type`, and normalization reduces it to `Bad`. The type-only call `cast(~Unit)` creates no instance, so it supplies a forged `Data` license for `Bad` and the Curry term inhabits `Empty`.

After checking, `book.tmps["cast"]` has zero entries. Renaming the binder to `~U` rejects the generic body with `expected Data, observed Type`. Adding a live `def live() -> Data: cast(~Unit)` creates `cast~0` and rejects that instance with the same mismatch. TL;DR I'm trying to define a simple co-algebra as I would in Lean, and maybe I'm just stupid but without copyable closures I can't figure out a nice way to do it (or at least a way without big tradeoffs in readability and reusability). My current impression is that being able to copy closures is a must-have, especially in my narrow use case of defining coalgebras and ITrees (interaction trees). Maybe sharing/publishing some good ways to defunctionalize common FP-brained patterns could help mitigate my (and other's skill issues). Or maybe it just needs to be more fundamentally solved at the language level.

<details>
<summary>
More details on what I'm trying to translate from Lean4 => Bend2 and why I care about coalgebras in the first place
</summary>


In Lean4:

```lean
inductive CoStep (Effect : Type → Type) (Res State : Type) : Type 1 where
  | pure (value : Res)
  | silent (next : State)
  | impure {X : Type} (operation : Effect X) (next : X → State)

structure CoFree (Effect : Type → Type) (Res : Type) : Type 1 where
  State : Type
  initial : State
  observe : State → CoStep Effect Res State
```

So the first issue is the `Effect` description, so for my use case I'll have to make to make the instance specialize or defunctionalize every instance I'm interested in which is already pretty ugly imo.

The next issue, and a more fundamental one to me is that there seems to be no reusable/generic way to define certain combinators like `iter`:

```lean
inductive IterStep (S E : Type) where
  | repeat : S → IterStep S E
  | exit : E → IterStep S E

private structure IterState (next : S → CoFree E (IterStep S A)) where
  index : S
  state : (next index).State

def CoFree.iter (start : S) (next : S → CoFree E (IterStep S A)) : CoFree E A where
  State := IterState next
  initial := ⟨start, (next start).initial⟩
  observe control :=
    match (next control.index).observe control.state with
    | .pure (.repeat index) => .silent ⟨index, (next index).initial⟩
    | .pure (.exit value) => .pure value
    | .silent state => .silent ⟨control.index, state⟩
    | .impure operation resume => .impure operation (fun answer => ⟨control.index, resume answer⟩)
```

because to "repeat" it needs to be able to call the body (`next`) at least once and then store it so the resulting object can be stepped again.

Taking a step back the reason I'm interested in coalgebras and ITrees in the first place is because I'm starting to see how (at least in Lean) they seem to let you define and write down specifications for effectful/non-deterministic processes in a very natural, almost imperative way which is super useful in my work to build and verify compilers.
</details>

Thank you for the measurements and the two clear asks. Here is where we landed.

**Base's `Array.map` is now a loop.** In 2.0.23 it walks the block with `Array.get`/`Array.set` into a fresh array instead of splitting and rebuilding the tree; on an M4 that is 16M U32 in about 10 ms instead of 166 ms, at a third of the memory. This is the same primitive set you have today: a loop of get/set compiles to one `for` of a block read and a block write, no allocation and no tree.

**`copy_range` and `swap2` stay out of Base**, because both are a few lines over the primitives, and Base is kept at a complexity cap. A get/set loop copies 16M U32 in 4-5 ms on one core (28 GB/s; a memcpy on the same machine does 2 ms, and the gap is that the emitted index is masked, which stops the vectorizer, not the loop itself). For `T: Data`:

```python
def Array.copy_range.put(~T: Data, +i: U32, dst: Array<T>, r: Array<T> & T) -> Array<T> & Array<T>:
  (src, x) = r
  (src, Array.set(T, dst, i, x))

def Array.copy_range.step(~T: Data, +i: U32, p: Array<T> & Array<T>) -> Array<T> & Array<T>:
  (src, dst) = p
  Array.copy_range.put(~T, i, dst, Array.get(T, src, i))

def Array.copy_range.go(~T: Data, +n: Nat, +i: U32, p: Array<T> & Array<T>) -> Array<T> & Array<T>:
  match n:
    case 0n:
      p
    case 1n+q:
      Array.copy_range.go(~T, q, U32.inc(i), Array.copy_range.step(~T, i, p))

def Array.copy_range(~T: Data, src: Array<T>, dst: Array<T>, +from: U32, +count: U32) -> Array<T> & Array<T>:
  Array.copy_range.go(~T, U32.to_nat(count), from, (src, dst))
```

`swap2` for `T: Data` needs no hole: get `i`, swap `j` (which returns the old value), set `i`; `i == j` is a no-op by itself:

```python
def Array.swap2.fin(~T: Data, +i: U32, r: Array<T> & T) -> Array<T>:
  (a, y) = r
  Array.set(T, a, i, y)

def Array.swap2.at(~T: Data, +i: U32, +j: U32, r: Array<T> & T) -> Array<T>:
  (a, x) = r
  Array.swap2.fin(~T, i, Array.swap(T, a, j, x))

def Array.swap2(~T: Data, a: Array<T>, +i: U32, +j: U32) -> Array<T>:
  Array.swap2.at(~T, i, j, Array.get(T, a, i))
```

For an affine `T: Type` the placeholder is not an accident of the API: every cell of a block holds a `T` and no cell is ever empty, so nothing can take a value out without putting one in; `Array.fork` is a second handle to the same cells and `Array.join` only drops one. A hole-free affine swap would be a runtime primitive that exchanges two cells. Your use cases (Fisher-Yates, in-place sort) are over numbers, where the Data version above is enough; if an affine case comes up in practice, reopen with it and we will look at the primitive. Note that these loops are written with `~T` (a template), not `-T`: an erased element type does not compile to a block loop on the C lane.

Moved here from #866's description, so that the PR describes the page target alone and this issue holds the WebGPU work in one place: first the six reasons a port of the Metal runtime cannot work in WebGPU, then the prototype runtime built around what WebGPU has, with its measurements. The three pages are live at <https://adrielsantana.github.io/metal-bending/>.

## Why a port cannot work

The natural next question is a WGSL lane for `!`, since WebGPU is the browser's only compute API now. I researched it against what the device runtime actually does (`bend_dev`: one persistent pipeline, ~4 dispatches per `!`, 64-bit terms, 32-bit atomics into the same heap, release/acquire handoffs through the heap between lanes of different threadgroups (a task pushed onto another lane's ring, a child's result read by the last child, which continues the parent), `coherent(device)` stores, a heap the CPU shares zero-copy). Each of these meets a WebGPU limit that is structural, not a porting detail:

1. **No 64-bit integers in WGSL.** Terms are `u64` (tag, 40-bit loc). Only `i32`/`u32` exist; the proposal has been open since 2019 ([gpuweb#273](https://github.com/gpuweb/gpuweb/issues/273)), no browser ships it, and Apple's position is that Mac2 Metal feature sets lack 64-bit math. Every term becomes a `vec2<u32>` with hand-rolled carries.
2. **Atomics are typed.** WGSL has only `atomic<u32>`/`atomic<i32>`, and a buffer cannot be bound both as `array<atomic<u32>>` and as plain storage ([buffer-binding aliasing](https://www.w3.org/TR/webgpu/)). The runtime's `a32_*` views into the 64-bit heap therefore mean the *whole heap* becomes atomics, every read an `atomicLoad` (a real RMW on the HLSL backend). Untyped atomics ([gpuweb#2377](https://github.com/gpuweb/gpuweb/issues/2377)) are still open.
3. **No device-scope fence for non-atomic data.** [WGSL §14.5](https://www.w3.org/TR/WGSL/#memory-model): storage atomics are relaxed, "all synchronization functions use the Workgroup memory scope", non-atomic storage accesses have workgroup scope. `storageBarrier()` cannot synchronize across workgroups ([gpuweb#3774](https://github.com/gpuweb/gpuweb/issues/3774), [#2980](https://github.com/gpuweb/gpuweb/issues/2980)); there is no `coherent(device)`, and wgpu confirmed no backend offers a device-scope barrier ([wgpu#7445](https://github.com/gfx-rs/wgpu/issues/7445)). The runtime's `a32 + FENCE` handoffs between threadgroups (`ring_push` with release, the join's `a32_sub_rel` then `a32_acq`) have no expression: every cross-workgroup word, payload included, must itself be an atomic with its own flag bits (what *Decoupled Fallback* does for prefix sums), or the handoff must cross a dispatch boundary.
4. **No forward progress across workgroups.** "You cannot assume more than one workgroup executes at a time" ([WGSL §15](https://www.w3.org/TR/WGSL/)). Today's device runtime never waits on another lane inside a dispatch (`WL_SPIN` is a leaf's loop polling the error flag; a join is finished by its last child), so it does not need this guarantee, but it sizes `CUBE_G` to the GPU's core count for occupancy, which WebGPU does not expose. Any port that added waiting would need an occupancy-discovery protocol plus bounded spins with a scalar fallback ([Sorensen et al., FSE'17](https://www.doc.ic.ac.uk/~afd/papers/2017/FSE.pdf); [Smith, Levien, Owens, SPAA'25](https://escholarship.org/content/qt0bk9z4bt/qt0bk9z4bt.pdf), which measures forward-progress failures on M1 Max and M3). A lane spinning forever is not a hang but a machine freeze on Apple Silicon ("Deathray", [write-up](https://auberon.xyz/blog/posts/deathray/), Apple declined to fix), and Chrome's GPU watchdog kills the device at 25 s on macOS, 15 s on Linux/Android ([source](https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/gpu/ipc/common/gpu_watchdog_timeout.h)).
5. **No shared heap.** `MAP_READ` may only pair with `COPY_DST`, `MAP_WRITE` with `COPY_SRC`; Dawn uses `Private` storage for everything else, with UMA copies an open issue since 2021 ([gpuweb#2388](https://github.com/gpuweb/gpuweb/issues/2388)). The zero-cost `!` of unified memory becomes `writeBuffer` + `mapAsync` per phase, and a round trip is measured in milliseconds even for 4 KB ([gpuweb#4432](https://github.com/gpuweb/gpuweb/issues/4432)). With ~4 dispatches per `!`, the fixed fee is where the Mandelbrot's whole frame is today.
6. **No transpiler gets there.** Tint's SPIR-V reader and the clang → clspv → Tint chain reject non-32-bit ints, pointers in structs and barrier non-uniformity ([HipScript's report](https://lights0123.com/blog/2025/01/07/hip-script/)); the Vulkan attempts on this runtime found the same. A lane would be a WGSL emitter written by hand for a runtime redesigned around 1–5, not a fourth dialect of the one source.

So it is a new device runtime, not a port. The six points stand as the reasons a port cannot work; the update below is that new runtime, prototyped by hand and measured, and it changes the conclusion I first wrote here (that the GPU's share stays on the desktop).

## A runtime built for WebGPU, measured

The result is not a port of the Metal runtime but a runtime written around what WebGPU has, and it runs three of the demos on the GPU in the browser: [Mandelbrot](https://adrielsantana.github.io/metal-bending/gpu_mandelbrot.html), [voxel raycaster](https://adrielsantana.github.io/metal-bending/gpu_voxel.html), [`demos/app_ray_tracer_3d` at 1024×768](https://adrielsantana.github.io/metal-bending/gpu_raytracer.html) (W/A/S/D, Q/E, arrows, the fps in the corner as in the original).

**Design.** Terms are `vec2<u32>` (x = loc, y = tag<<24 | aux<<8; a loc fits 32 bits in the browser). A task node is `[args.., cont, (pend, idx)]` as in the C, with the pending count in a separate `array<atomic<u32>>`, so the heap stays a plain `array<u32>`. The only fence between lanes is a dispatch boundary: one indirect dispatch per fork level grows the frontier (a fork pushes its four children onto the next queue), one dispatch works each subtree sequentially on a lane (the runtime's own `seq` path: `WL_FRAME`, the K continuations on an explicit interleaved stack, the join segment, `FID_EXIT`), one dispatch per join level folds back, one walks the quadtree into pixels (`window_pix`), a fullscreen triangle blits. `task_deliver` writes into the parent's node and `atomicSub`s the count; the last child pushes the parent onto the next queue instead of continuing it. Three queues rotate (in, out, one being reset) so a kernel never writes the indirect-args buffer it was launched from, and an `atomicMax` on the workgroup count at each push makes a flip kernel unnecessary. 15 to 21 dispatches a frame in one command buffer, nothing read back. So: no u64, no untyped atomics, no device-scope fence, no forward progress and no shared heap needed. Points 1 to 6 above stand for a port; they are not a wall for a runtime built this way.

| ms per frame | WebAssembly, 10 threads | WebGPU |
|---|---|---|
| Mandelbrot 512² | 4–5 | 0.31 |
| Voxel raycaster 512² (`fork!(7n)` to 4×4 tiles, a DDA of 96 steps per ray) | 42 (24 fps) | 1.8 |
| `demos/app_ray_tracer_3d`, 512×384 | ≤ 16 (60 fps, capped) | 0.7 |
| `demos/app_ray_tracer_3d`, 1024×768 | 53 (19 fps) | 2.4 |

GPU time of the compute pass from timestamp queries, median of 100 frames submitted back to back, Chrome 153 on the M5 (`--enable-webgpu-developer-features`, so the timestamps are not quantized). The image is checked against a JavaScript rendering of the same pixel function: the Mandelbrot differs on 10 of 262144 pixels by one escape step (a fused multiply-add), the raycaster on 2 (a tie between two faces, the class of difference `REPORT.md` in metal-bending already records for Metal), the ray tracer on none. Seven fork levels (16384 lanes, then a sequential subtree per lane) is the sweet spot; every level as its own dispatch, with no sequential pass, is 4.5x slower, and three fork levels 18x. In a 60 Hz loop the GPU clocks down between frames and the pass reads 3 to 5x longer; the table is the throughput.

**What is generic, what is by hand.** The scheduler, the heap, the joins and the raster are one file ([`rt.js`](https://github.com/AdrielSantana/metal-bending/blob/gh-pages/rt.js), ~300 lines of WGSL and ~150 of JS) shared unchanged by the three pages. What each page adds is the leaf (the Mandelbrot's pixel, the raycaster's tile with its 2×2 collapse, `Fly.over`) and the rule for the children's arguments, translated by hand from the Bend source, since there is no WGSL emitter. That emitter is the real work: the leaf and segment code from Bend's IR to WGSL (`Bool.pick` as `select`, `F32.to_u32` as the saturating `u32()`, fuel recursion as a bounded loop, the `!` frontier as the dispatch plan above). It does not fit `comp.ts` at its budget, so it would be a file of its own or a fork. The prototype's allocator is a per-frame arena, enough for a `!` whose result is drawn (all four demos here), not for state kept on the device heap across frames.
