`_` is never escaped, so `a-b` → `a_2d_b`, the same as `name_tt("a_2d_b")`). Def names are made unique
afterwards by `fresh`; labels aren't.

**1. A group selector with two colliding members is unparsable.** A mutually recursive group whose
members are `L.k` (from `a-b.bend`, imported as `L`) and a local `a_2d_b.k` gets the selector enum
`<a_2d_b.k, a_2d_b.k>`:

```python
# ---- a-b.bend ----
import Base

law k:
  for n: Nat
  Nat

# ---- main.bend ----
import Base
import ./a-b.bend as L

def keep(n: Nat, -m: Nat) -> Nat:
  n

def a_2d_b.k(n: Nat) -> Nat:
  keep(n, L.k(n))

def L.k(n):
  match n:
    case 0n:
      0n
    case 1n+p:
      a_2d_b.k(p)
```

A `~` def means the set of its instances, one per closed argument; with an empty type there are none, so `main`'s zero roots were correct, and emitting the body at an opaque constant with no model makes a vacuous def that names `v` (e.g. `absurd(v)`) fail `--verdict`.

The real gap is that `--verdict` trusts `root_cols`' enumeration to cover the law. The follow-up will emit, for a root with a finite `~` parameter, the law's own universal statement as a λ-match dispatching to its instances, so the kernel checks the coverage (and for an empty type checks `λ{}` directly).

Code review of f54dc5fc. The fixpoint itself looks correct: answers only grow, a recursive `spec_of` call can't happen, reads are recorded correctly, and the loop over the `Set` worklist stops. There are five findings. Only the first was confirmed by running it; the other four are about speed and test coverage, and weren't measured.

**1. A type that recurses at a growing argument now hangs where main fails cleanly (confirmed).** `safe.ts:387`

```python
type S<n: Type, m: Type> is Kind(qof(n)):
  S1{s: S<List<m>, n>}
```

- **main:** `-o` exits 0 with `S: a kind that depends on a run-time value`.
- **this PR:** `m` is now specialized, so `S` is instantiated at `(S~n, S~m)`, `(List S~m, S~n)`, `(List S~n, List S~m)`, and so on. It was stopped after 60 s (exit 124). `--verdict` goes through the same path.
- **What to fix:** `item_ref` has no limit on how many instances it makes, and the one-parameter form (`T<n>` with a field `T<List<n>>`) already hangs on main. So the real fix is a limit, or a check for growing instance keys, in `item_ref`/`e.todo`. This PR only makes more books reach that hang.

**2. `spec_of` allocates on every call, even when cached.** `safe.ts:353`

It builds a `Set`, a `Map` and three closures on each call. It's on hot paths:
- `args()` calls it for every application of a named item;
- `root_cols` calls it once per parameter;
- `group_emit` calls it per member.

Since `spec_of` never calls itself, every cached answer is final, so returning the cached value first is safe:

```ts
const sp = e.spec.get(k);
if (sp !== undefined) return sp;
```

**3. Every self-recursive datatype with a specialized parameter is computed twice.** `safe.ts:366`

A constructor's return type reads the type itself with its own parameters, which can't change the answer. This is the PR table's 301→601 on the chain and 202→403 on the fan-in. Two ways to avoid the second pass for almost every datatype:
- don't record the type as its own reader when it reads itself with parameter j's variable at position j;
- or solve each strongly connected component once.

**4. Each recomputation redoes work that doesn't depend on the fixpoint.** `safe.ts:386`

It lowers the telescope and every constructor type again, calls `tele_unbind` again, and runs `is_qnt(term_wnf(…))` on every parameter type, though only `got` changes between passes. Computing the lowered terms and the `is_qnt`/template mask once per item removes that cost for datatypes in a cycle with many constructors or large parameter types.

**5. The regression test is only guarded by `gates/safe.ts`.** `tests/check/spec_cycle.bend:27`

Minimal pair (only the `~f` domain differs, the defaulted arm `x` is identical):

**Rejected** (Bool domain — `x` free in the default arm caught):

```python
def app(~f: Bool -> Nat) -> Nat:
  f(True{})

def g(x: Nat) -> Nat:
  app(~{\{False: 0n; x} : Bool -> Nat})
```
> expected : a template applied to closed ~ arguments (x is a variable here, not comptime: pass it at run time)

**Accepted** (`--check-only` green): Unit domain, same open default arm:

```python
def app(~f: Unit -> Nat) -> Nat:
  f(Unit{})

def g(x: Nat) -> Nat:
  app(~{\{Unit: 0n; x} : Unit -> Nat})

def h(x: Bool) -> Nat:
  app(~{\{Unit: 0n; x} : Unit -> Nat})
```

So a free run-time variable in a **defaulted** arm passes the guard when the domain is a single-label ADT (where the default is unreachable at run time) and fails when the domain has more labels — the guard seems to key on arm reachability rather than on the argument actually being closed. The `term_key` collision in my report above then rides on top of this: both `g` and `h` submit "open-but-accepted" arguments that serialize identically, and `h` reuses `g`'s `app~0` without its own instantiation ever being checked.

```

```

i.e. the kernel refuses the emitted book that carries the dangling `x` — so the leak currently lands on the safe side, but the specialization cache itself is unsound: a `Bool` value flows through a `Nat`-typed spine (`app(~f: Unit -> Nat)` applied with an argument whose default arm is `x : Bool` yields `h(True{})` computed as `True{}` at type `Nat`). **Where `-O1 -g` falls short is stepping through a foreign effect's own C.** The case behind this PR is a TLS client I'm writing as a foreign effect:
- it loads OpenSSL 3 with `dlopen`, so a plain `bend -o` builds it with nothing added to the link line;
- it drives `SSL_connect`, `SSL_read` and `SSL_write` on the socket's own fd;
- on `WANT_READ` or `WANT_WRITE` it parks with `io_wait_on`.

Its bugs live in that C: how `SSL_get_error` and `errno` are read after a failed call, a truncation told apart from a reset, a fatal error that must not reach `SSL_shutdown`. The JS lane runs the `.js` twin, not this C, so a native debug build is the only place to step through it. With the sockets and the effect in one program, main can't build it at `-O0` ("ran out of registers during register allocation in function 'WL_FID_ENTER'", clang 22.1.8).

At `-O1 -g`, I set a break in the read path right after `SSL_read` returns, while the server's bytes are still arriving. Against `openssl s_server` on loopback:

```
-O1 -g (main)                          -O0 -g (this PR)
n      = <optimized out>               n      = -1
sslerr = 2                             sslerr = 2    (SSL_ERROR_WANT_READ)
syserr = <optimized out>               syserr = 11   (EAGAIN)

#0 tls_recv_more (e=..., w=...)        #0 tls_recv_more (e=..., w=...)
#1 io_exec (e=..., w=...)              #1 tls_recv_run (e=..., f=0x7fffffffb8e0, w=...)
                                       #2 io_exec (e=..., w=...)
```

`n` is `SSL_read`'s return and `syserr` the `errno` taken right after it. Those are the two values that tell a reset from a truncation, and the ones a bug that reads `errno` too late gets wrong. At `-O1`, both are gone, and so is the effect's own entry frame.

The same shape can be reproduced from the repo's own tests: append `foreign_shared.bend`'s `Tree`, `shared.make`, `tree.sum`, `wrap` and `both` to `tests/io/tcp_poll.bend`, and print `both(shared.make(4))` in its main before the listener.
- On main, `-O0 -g` fails the same way.
- At `-O1 -g`, a break in `shared_make_at` shows `depth` as `<optimized out>` in every caller frame, and `f` and `w` in `shared_make_run`.
- `foreign_shared` on its own, at `-O1 -g`, even shows a wrong value. The same `next` pointer is passed down every call, and frame #0 shows it as `0x7fffffffb68c`, but two frames of the backtrace show it as `0x200000000000000`.

**On keeping one convention:**
- **The default convention is already a supported runtime.** Since cd3366a9, `PRESERVE` is empty wherever clang lacks either attribute, and `cc_find` takes clang 14 for a CPU build. So `bend -o` with clang 14–18 builds exactly what this PR gives a `-O0` build.
- **A `preserve_none` failure like the one `rp` pads around shows up when clang builds the C.** Per 386b7fc1, "regalloc fails on any dynamic jump with 6+ defined words". That shows at `-O1` and up, where this PR changes nothing: on current main, the assembly at `-O1`, `-O2` and `-O3` is byte-identical with and without it. A debug build isn't where you'd find it, and today a `-O0` build of a program that size can't be made at all.

If you'd still rather a `-O0` build be a deliberate choice, I can make it opt-in instead: a define that drops the attributes, so a plain `-O0` build fails as it does now. And if a debug build isn't something you want to support, closing it is fine too.

**The compiled lanes already use a single compare.** Base's `Nat.min` and `Nat.max` compile to the `nat_min` and `nat_max` intrinsics, so C and JS emit no recursion. For

```
def main() -> Nat:
  lo = Nat.min(Nat.mul(12000000n, 11000000n), Nat.mul(10000000n, 10000000n))
  hi = Nat.max(Nat.mul(12000000n, 11000000n), Nat.mul(10000000n, 10000000n))
  Nat.add(lo, hi)
```

the JS lane emits `const _lo_0 = (_x_0 < _x_1 ? _x_0 : _x_1);` and `const _hi_0 = (_x_2 > _x_3 ? _x_2 : _x_3);`, and both C and JS print `232000000000000n`. Past 2^48-1, a compiled Nat fail-stops by design: "A Nat past 2^48-1, or an array past block class 31, fail-stops (#779)".

**The overflow is in `bend file.bend`.** That command evaluates a pure `main` with the checker's evaluator, not with the compiled code, and it overflows on any large Nat arithmetic, not just `min` and `max`: `Nat.add(4000000000n, 3000000000n)` and `Nat.mul(12000000n, 11000000n)` overflow there too. That's "The checker is not optimal: some terms are exponential or overflow (#993, #1075)", which asks not to open an issue per overflow. Thanks for the careful write-up. The crash on g4 is real, and this PR does fix it, but I feel like the new `group_of` patches a symptom instead of the cause.

The cause. refs (safe.ts:1111) collects every Ref in a body, including those inside erased arguments. Only later and group_new call it, so a dead reference can form a group, pick a group's leader, or reroute a call. The candidate loop in group_of and the group_new in item_emit both work around that. Neither stops dead references from shaping groups.

The new test shows this. Its header says dead references "neither add group members nor select a group's leader". Yet h names L only inside keep's erased -p, and it still ends up a member: L.group gets an .h arm, and the member law relies on that.

I was thinking on something like make grouping count only live references. That is option 3 in #1212. A dead forward reference doesn't need a group: item_ref already emits a dead name lazily, and the kernel accepts a dead forward reference. So only live cycles should form groups, like base's String.cmp / String.cmp.fin. Then later(k)[0] can't be an unrelated def, group_of can go back to its one-liner, and you don't need the candidate loop or the item_emit change.

I'm not completely sure this is the best option, but I think it's a good exploration path.

What has to happen:
- refs (or a sibling used only for grouping) skips erased argument positions. Those are the quantity-0 args of an App and anything under an erased binder, the same positions args treats as dead.
- group_of returns to group_new(e, later(e, k)[0] ?? k). If a case remains where k isn't in the group it gets, raise oos(...) there. Don't pick a group silently.

- conversion between two such aliases

Bounding each walker is possible, but it means patching every walker for one family of inputs, which is what WONTFIX.txt asks us not to do ("each layer covers one more family"). It also fails closed: nothing is accepted that shouldn't be, and the kernel is never reached.

These aliases also have almost no practical use. Inhabiting Sink or a Mealy machine M = U32 -> Pair(U32, M) in live code needs a self-call that doesn't descend, which bend2 rejects. Only trivial terms like x => x : F get through. The useful negative and recursive types are written as datatypes, which are nominal, don't unfold, and check fine today, --verdict included:

type F is Type:
  MkF{f: F -> F}

def g() -> F:
  MkF{x => x}

I see how it can be annoying for writing math. We may add a global checker timeout later, and we may revisit recursive aliases themselves with Taelin, either supporting them across all walkers or rejecting them up front with a clear error.

A review turned up some correctness problems. Each one below has a reproduction on both the C and JS lanes, and none of them is caught by the new tests.

1. An early-woken channel try_ leaves its timer parked, which hides deadlocks and slows the loop (effs/chan.c:96,108, effs/chan.js:58)

When a try_ waiter is woken before its deadline, its timer is only disarmed, so it stays in io_park (C) or io.waits (JS) for the full ms. That breaks two things:
- Deadlock detection. The deadlock checks (comp.ts:5974, comp.ts:6382) can't fire while the dead timer is parked. For example, a fiber does Chan.try_recv(c, 6000), gets answered at once, then blocks in Chan.recv on a channel nobody sends to. main reports the deadlock in 0.01 s; this branch takes 6 s on both lanes. With ms = 4294967295 it hangs for about 49.7 days instead of exiting 1. That contradicts tests/io/deadlock.bend and the GUIDE.
- Throughput. A consumer doing try_recv(c, 30000) per message took 31.7 s and 266 MB on C for 8M messages, against 0.5 s and 1.7 MB when the timer is unlinked on wake. With one fiber parked in a blocking UDP.recv_from, the cost grows quadratically, because io_park_add walks past every dead timer. On JS, 1M messages took 12.1 s and 1.45 GB.

This came in with 8c151b9a. At 311881bb the timer was unlinked on wake, and the same programs ran at blocking speed. A park entry that can be cancelled with an O(1) unlink would fix both problems. It would also stop overloading the waiter's made field as both the timer pointer and the "is try_" flag.

2. C and JS disagree when a try_ deadline and a wake land in the same loop pass (effs/chan.js:50)

On C, chan_late removes the timed-out waiter inside io_wait itself. On JS, the waiter's io_wake only joins the run queue, so a fiber already queued ahead of it still finds the expired waiter in row.wait and hands it Ready. Take a capacity-0 channel. Fiber S does IO.sleep(20) then Chan.send(c, 7). The main fiber does IO.sleep(0), then Chan.try_recv(c, 20), then a Chan.recv if it got Wait. C prints A: wait / A: then got 7 / S: sent. JS prints S: sent / A: ready got 7, on every run. So JS delivers to a waiter whose deadline already passed, which contradicts the Poll docs. Any test that hits this ordering passes on one lane and fails on the other.

3. C heap leaks: a result is built before the outcome is known, then overwritten
- effs/udp_recv_from.c:17 builds Wait{Unit} up front and replaces it whenever a datagram or error arrives. That leaks 8 bytes on every received datagram, including in the blocking UDP.recv_from, which doesn't leak on main. Over 3M datagrams, max RSS reached 25.8 MB, against a flat 1.8 MB with the fix. The netcode relay's Server.loop would grow about 290 MB/hour at 10k datagrams/s.
- effs/udp_send_to.c:19 and effs/tcp_send.c:22 build Done{Unit} up front and replace it on failure, and udp_send_to.c also replaces it on Wait. That leaks 8 bytes per failed send and per UDP.try_send_to that answers Wait. 4M failing sends reached 33.7 MB against 1.7 MB.

Building only the branch that is actually returned fixes all three, which is what io_res did on main.

4. UDP.recv_from with max = 0 doesn't fail with EINVAL (effs/udp_recv_from.c:29, and the JS version)

base.bend now says a max of 0 "fails with EINVAL, as in every receive below", but the UDP effects never check for it:
- With a datagram queued, UDP.recv_from(s, 0) answers Done{(127.0.0.1, p, "")} and the datagram is silently lost.
- On a quiet socket on macOS, try_recv_from(s, 0, 50) answers at once with Ready{Done{("0.0.0.0", 0, "")}}, a datagram that was never sent.

The f[1] == 0 guard in tcp_recv_start can be copied over.

5. The io_tcp_echos demo's proofs no longer type-check (demos/io_tcp_echos/LAWS.bend:10,16)

echo_step now takes Result<…, Maybe<String>>, but the laws still pass Done{SCon{c, t}} and Done{""}. bend demos/io_tcp_echos/PROOF.bend --check-only fails with expected: Maybe<&1, String> / observed: String. Changing them to Done{Some{SCon{c, t}}} and Done{None{}} restores main's result. The (an empty recv) comment at line 12 is also out of date. No gate checks demos, so CI won't catch this.


Non-blocking
- Repeated try_ code. The Ready wrapping and the deadline logic are copied into every effect on both lanes, in a few slightly different forms (at != 0, by != 0, w->time ?). The leaks in item 3 come from one of these copies. Helpers such as io_ready(e, at, r) and io_after(ms) next to io_res would keep them in one place.
- Repeated error builder. The Fail{((code, msg), rest)} payload repeats io_fail's body three times in C, and JS patches .error in three places. An io_err for the (code, msg) pair, plus an optional rest argument on JS's io_fail, would make each site one expression.
- send_bytes walks its list twice. tcp_send_bytes_start checks for values above 255 in its own pass before io_cbuf walks the list again, costing about 20–25% more CPU on large lists. An io_cbuf that checks before consuming the list, as JS io_unlist already does, would remove this. It would also remove the unexplained strdup("-") host workaround in udp_send_to_start.
- Small things in chan.c. Wait{rest} is built in two places, where JS has a single chan_rest. The last ternary arm in chan_cut assigns *q to itself. The made = 0 stores after a wake are never read.

The design covers everything #1162 was for, and more (the `rest` on a send and on a partial write). Below is a Linux x86-64 run of 987d60d6: the tests, the cost, and how @Lorenzobattistela's points show up there.

**Tests.** On the check, interpreted, JS and C lanes, these print their `#|` lines: `chan_try`, `tcp_try`, `tcp_try_bytes`, `tcp_try_recv`, `udp_try`, `udp_try_recv_from`, and the changed `chan_close_send`, `tcp_bytes`, `tcp_recv_max_zero`, `tcp_short_recv`, `udp_bad_address`, `tcp_loopback`. I did not run the whole tree.

**Cost.** 1M operations, 5 runs each, f2cc47cd against this head:

| 1M × | f2cc47cd | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| blocking `Chan.send` + `Chan.recv`, both ready | C 104–107 ms, JS 575–600 ms | C 108–109 ms, JS 587–608 ms |
| `try_recv(c, 0)` on an empty channel | (#1162's `try_recv`: C 51 ms, JS 300 ms) | C 52–56 ms, JS 283–297 ms |

The step that does not wait costs what #1162's did, and the blocking path pays about 3% on C and 0–4% on JS, close to the spread between runs.

**The review's points on Linux.**

- **1, the parked timer, throughput.** One producer, a channel with no room, and a consumer that takes each message with `Chan.try_recv(c, 30000)`, on C:

  | messages | `Chan.recv` | `Chan.try_recv(c, 30000)` |
  |---|---|---|
  | 300k | | 0.09 s, 24 MB |
  | 500k | | 1.9 s, 35 MB |
  | 700k | | 30.1 s, 40 MB |
  | 1M | 0.11 s, 14 MB | 41–46 s, 41–43 MB |

  With `ms` 5000 the 700k run takes 5.3 s, so past some count of parked timers the run lasts as long as the deadline. On JS, 1M take 62 s and 1.08 GB, against 0.72 s and 90 MB with `Chan.recv`.
- **1, the deadlock report.** A fiber answered at once by `Chan.try_recv(c, 6000)` that then blocks for good is reported after 6.0 s on C and JS, against 2 ms without the `try_`. This is the cost the description names.
- **2, C and JS disagree.** His program prints `A: wait` / `A: then got 7` / `S: sent` on C and `S: sent` / `A: ready got 7` on JS, three runs out of three each.
- **3, the leaks.** They don't show here. Max RSS stays at 13.9 MB on both f2cc47cd and this head over 3M `UDP.send_to` + `UDP.recv_from` on loopback, and over 4M `UDP.send_to` that fail with EINVAL. My programs may miss his shape.
- **4, UDP `max` 0.** With two datagrams queued, `UDP.recv_from(s, 0)` answers `Done` with `""` and the first datagram is gone, on C and JS. f2cc47cd does the same, so the behavior is not new; what is new is Base's comment that every receive fails with EINVAL.
- **5, the demo's proofs.** `bend demos/io_tcp_echos/PROOF.bend --check-only` fails at `echoes_data`, as he says.

**Fit.** The shapes match what a networked program needs: a receive with a deadline is `TCP.try_recv`, a byte-level one is `TCP.try_recv_bytes`, and a send with a deadline hands back what the kernel did not take. Moving code off `TCP.poll` is one line per call. The reserved `Ready` and `Wait` names are the one cost to existing programs worth stating in the changelog.

JS and the interpreter printed `S: sent / A: ready got 7`; now every lane prints `A: wait / A: then got 7 / S: sent`.

Thanks for this. Comparing the path's types with term_compare is the right fix for the W<F> overflow.

But four files that pass --verdict on main fail on this branch:

1. Rebound model λs freeze their inner variables (safe.ts:456). The subst swaps in level d but turns every other variable into a fixed B.Var(k, i). That includes variables bound inside the body, so a nested model λ ignores its argument once the model book applies it. Returning undefined for o.i > d fixes it.

```
law L:
  for ~f: @A: Type -> A -> A
  for ~h: @B: Type -> @c: Nat -> @b: B -> {f(B, b) == b : B}
  for x: Nat
  {f(Nat, x) == x : Nat}

def L(f, h, x):
  h(Nat, 0n, x)
main: ALL PROOFS CHECK. This PR: no model for L~h. Change the law to {f(B, b) == c : B} and the search instead finds a {==} that the kernel then rejects.
```

2. The sort orders all constructors by field count, not only nullary ones first (safe.ts:464). A recursive constructor with one field now runs before a finite leaf with two fields and uses up the whole budget before the leaf is tried:

```
type G<-A: Type> is Type:
  Leaf{a: A, b: A}
  Grow{rest: G<Pair(A, A)>}

def reflexive(~n: G<Nat>) -> {n == n : G<Nat>}:
  {==}
main: ALL PROOFS CHECK in 0.07 s. This PR: no model after 4.7 s. Moving only the nullary constructors first (Number(a.n > 0) - Number(b.n > 0)) fixes this case.
```

3. Any reordering changes which models existing files get. A ~ law that held of the old first-constructor model can stop holding:

```
type Shape is Data:
  Rect{w: Nat, h: Nat}
  Circle{r: Nat}

law shape_t:
  for ~mk: Nat -> Shape
  for ~ok: @x: Nat -> {is_rect(mk(x)) == True{} : Bool}
  for x: Nat
  {is_rect(mk(x)) == True{} : Bool}
main models mk as λx. Rect{0n, 0n} and checks. This PR picks Circle{0n}, so ok has no model. Even a nullary-first order changes types like Has{x} | Nothing{}.
```

4. The depth limit of 128 rejects finite models that main finds. def reflexive(~v: Vec(130n)) -> {v == v : Vec(130n)}, with Vec(n) defined as Unit at zero and Nat & Vec(p) at a successor, checks on main in 0.07 s and is out of scope here.

Run time. The budget counts visits, but each visit runs a full term_compare against every entry on the path. The G case above makes about 466k comparisons per attempt, and Vec(120n) takes 0.51 s against main's 0.07 s. Two cheaper alternatives:
- skip path entries with a different head (A.k !== F.k);
- skip the path scan when h !== null.

Also, a failing ~ constant is searched in root_cols and again in def_emit, so each "no model" pays for all four attempts.

Suggestion. Instead of one shared budget plus a reorder, try iterative deepening: search in declaration order with a depth limit that grows each round, under the same total budget. That finds the shallowest model, keeps every model main picks today (fixing 2 and 3), and still ends Nest/Grow. It should also make the rebase with #1263, which changes the same function, simpler.

The fix is to check each PR combined with current main right before it lands, not just its own branch. GitHub can do that if the gate runs there instead of on someone's machine. The repo gate only needs git, bun and ttok, so unlike the test and perf gates (which need Metal and the minis) it can run on GitHub's own Linux machines. It takes two pieces:

1. A workflow file that runs the gate and reports a pass/fail check on the PR. The `merge_group` trigger is what lets it run on the merge queue's combined branch (below):

```yaml
# .github/workflows/repo-gate.yml
name: repo-gate
on:
  pull_request:
  merge_group:
jobs:
  repo-gate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: oven-sh/setup-bun@v2
      - run: pipx install ttok
      - run: bun gates/repo.ts
```

2. A repo setting that a repo admin turns on for `main`, under Settings > Rules > [Rulesets](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-rulesets/about-rulesets):
   - "Require status checks to pass", with `repo-gate` added, so a PR can't merge while that check is failing or missing.
   - "Require merge queue" ([merge queue docs](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/configuring-pull-request-merges/managing-a-merge-queue)).

With the queue on, nobody merges directly. "Merge when ready" puts the PR in the queue, GitHub builds a temporary branch of current main plus every PR queued ahead plus this one, and runs the check on that. If it passes, the PR merges; if not, it's dropped from the queue and main is untouched. For #1269 that branch would have been main with the five newer merges plus #1269, at 64,250 tokens, so it would have failed instead of landing.

The simpler setting is "Require branches to be up to date before merging" instead of the queue: a PR that's behind main has to be updated and rechecked before it can merge. That gives the same guarantee, but with 10+ merges a day everyone keeps rebasing and waiting on reruns, which the queue does for them.

Bend had exactly this kind of setup (a checks workflow with a `merge_group` trigger) until c36597a2 replaced the Bend 1 tree, so this would be bringing one job back, plus one allow-list line for the workflow file. Happy to send the workflow as a PR if you want it; the ruleset needs a repo admin.

A direction not yet raised here: give each segment its exact width instead of one program-wide bank with a cap. From the experiments below, that isn't expressible in C, and LLVM IR looks like the only way to get it.

### Motivating example

The limit applies to the *type* of a value that is live across a call, not to how much data it holds. Any record of one-word fields hits it once it is live across one call:

```bend
type State is Data:
  S{f0: U32, f1: U32, ..., f259: U32}

def bump(+n: U32) -> U32:
  U32.add(n, 1)

def rebuild(+k: U32, s: State) -> State:
  match s:
    case S{+f0, ..., +f259}: S{U32.add(f0, k), ..., U32.add(f259, k)}

# s is live across the call to bump.
def step(s: State, +n: U32) -> State:
  rebuild(bump(n), s)
```

The interpreter answers (`42` for `main = first(step(S{0, ..., 259}, 41))`). The C build refuses with `an arity over 255`; on 2.0.25 the limit is 255, and #1068 later moved it to 247. In our case the record is the state of a composed state machine. Composing machines pairs their states, so the width adds up across components while every component stays small. Today the options are to box the state by hand, which is acceptable for us only because every step waits on IO, or to reorder evaluation as @ajoslin did. A compute-bound program pays an allocation and an indirection per step for a limit that comes from the calling convention.

### Why a cap is needed at all

Every segment shares `WL_SIG` because the host jumps between segments with `musttail`, and C's `musttail` requires identical prototypes. I checked this with clang 21.1.8 (arm64) under the default convention, `preserve_none` and `swiftasynccall`. All three reject different parameter counts:

```c
__attribute__((noinline, preserve_none)) u64 g(u64 a, u64 b, u64 c);
__attribute__((noinline, preserve_none)) u64 f(u64 a) { __attribute__((musttail)) return g(a, a, a); }
// error: cannot perform a tail call to function 'g' because its signature is incompatible
//        with the calling function (expected 1 but has 3)
```

The spill proposed above keeps the shared bank and moves the excess through memory. That works, but it keeps a cap (whose value is a tuning choice per lane), a second code path for the segments past it, and a program-wide signature set by its widest segment.

### LLVM IR can express exact widths

LLVM's `tailcc` convention has the callee pop its own arguments, and it guarantees tail calls between functions of *different* signatures. With the same clang 21.1.8 (arm64):

- a 2-argument and a 15-argument `tailcc` function calling each other 10^8 times (15 is past arm64's 8 argument registers, so some arguments go on the stack): correct result at `-O0` and `-O2`, no stack growth;
- a 2-argument and a **300-argument** `tailcc` function calling each other 10^7 times: correct result at `-O0` and `-O2` (checked against an independent computation).

```llvm
define tailcc i64 @narrow(i64 %n, i64 %acc) {
  %z = icmp eq i64 %n, 0
  br i1 %z, label %out, label %go
out:
  ret i64 %acc
go:
  %m = sub i64 %n, 1
  %r = tail call tailcc i64 @wide(i64 %m, i64 %acc, i64 1, i64 2, ..., i64 13)
  ret i64 %r
}
define tailcc i64 @wide(i64 %n, i64 %acc, i64 %a, ..., i64 %m) {
  ; ...
  %r = tail call tailcc i64 @narrow(i64 %n, i64 %acc2)
  ret i64 %r
}
```

So the host lane could emit each segment at its exact width, with no cap, no shared bank and no spill path. A segment's cost would follow its own width. The parts that would need design rather than a constant:

- **Unknown calls** (`Clo~apply`, `wl_tab`), where the callee's width is known only at run time. The usual answer is GHC's eval/apply ("Making a fast curry", Marlow and Peyton Jones). Known calls jump to the exact-width entry. Unknown calls go through a uniform entry per segment that unpacks from the closure node, which already holds the captures.
- **Suspend and resume** (`WL_SAVE`/`WL_TAKE`, joins, IO parking) would save exactly the suspended segment's width, which the emitter already records.
- **Tables and buffers** (`FID_ARITY_T`, `Term fs[256]`) widen to match, which also closes the `u8` truncation class @aldeni found.
- **The device lane** is one `switch` per kernel with per-lane registers. It has no per-segment signatures, so it would still need a register budget and a spill past it. The cap only goes away on the host.

### Caveats

- This is a move from emitting C to emitting LLVM IR, at least for the segment and call layer, which is a large change.
- I could **not** reproduce the clang crashes reported here and in #1233 with synthetic code. A shared 300-word `preserve_none`/`musttail` bank in C also built and ran correctly on clang 21.1.8 (arm64). So I have no evidence either way that exact widths avoid those crashes, which seem to depend on the emitted code, not only on the width.
- I haven't measured `tailcc`'s cost against the current shared bank. Given @aldeni's measurement that a wide bank costs about nothing on clang 22 (x86-64), the case for this is structural (no cap, no truncation class, no program-wide coupling to the widest segment), not performance.

In the theory, ! is erased, so f(x) == f!(x) holds by refl for any f. At runtime, that holds for integer code and for F32 add, sub, mul, div and sqrt, which IEEE 754 requires to be correctly rounded, so every target gives the same bits. It doesn't hold for the transcendental functions (sin, cos, tan, exp, log, pow, ...). IEEE 754 doesn't require correct rounding for those, so each target uses its own math library (libm on the host, CUDA's sinf, Metal's fast::), and they can differ in the last bit. A comparison on that bit, like the one in decide, can then take different branches for f(x) and f!(x).

The same bits on every target would need one shared software implementation of these functions, which would be slower on the GPU.

## What was left

Once a cycle specializes its parameters correctly, a specialized parameter can recur at a bigger argument each time, and `item_ref` names instances without end:

| file | main | f54dc5fc | f77b1c3d |
|---|---|---|---|
| `S<n, m>` with a field `S<List<m>, n>` | out of scope | hangs | out of scope |
| `T<n>` with a field `T<List<n>>` | hangs | hangs | out of scope |
| `U<n: Nat>` with a field `U<1n+n>` | hangs | hangs | out of scope |
| `A<n>` → `B<List<n>>` → `A<m>` | out of scope | hangs | out of scope |
| `def f(c: Nat, n: Type, -A: Kind(qof(n)))` calling `f(p, List<n>, Unit)` | stack overflow | stack overflow | out of scope |

The reason given is `a specialized argument that grows at each instance of S`. The def case shows that growth also comes from def bodies, not only from types, so a check over types alone isn't enough.

## The change

**`spec_of` is a reachability.** The specialized parameters are the least set closed under the rules, which is graph reachability:
- **Seeds:** a Quant or `~` parameter, or a variable that a kind reads.
- **Flows:** an edge from `h`'s parameter `i` to `r`'s parameter `j` when `r`'s `j` sits inside an argument at `h`'s `i`.

Each item's types are walked once to collect seeds and flows, and the seeds then spread along the flows. The answer can't depend on declaration order, and no item is computed twice. This replaces the redo worklist and covers findings 2–4 above:
- `spec_of` returns a cached answer first.
- A type that reads itself is no longer computed a second time.
- Nothing is lowered or unbound again.

Computation counts are back to main's (chain of 300 types 303, fan-in with 400 fields 404).

**`item_ref` stops growing instances.** It records which instance named each new one. A new instance is out of scope when its arguments *hold* those of an instance of the same item above it on that chain. *Holds* is a homeomorphic embedding: `S~n` is held in `List<S~n>`, and a number or a string literal holds a smaller one.
- Every endless chain of instances must contain such a pair (Kruskal's theorem), so every case in the table ends.
- A finite cycle like `S<m, n>` has no such pair, so it still goes out.
- A shrinking index has none either: `V<3n>` with a field `V<Nat.sub(n, 1n)>` goes out as its 4 instances.
- A bit per item along each chain skips the walk when the item isn't above. Without it, the walk took 10.7M steps on the fan-in; on the corpus it now takes 0.

- `tests/check/spec_cycle.bend` now also uses the cycles at closed arguments (`B<Nat>`, `S<Nat, Bool>`, `C<Nat, Bool>`).

The same question seen from the JS lane's exports (2.0.35): such a character cannot be built there, but an export receives it from its host, and two of them stored one after the other in a `String` read back as one character.

### What you did

Bend 2.0.35 (`79df8d9c`), Bun 1.3.14, macOS arm64.

```python
import Base

def reverseOnto(s: String, acc: String) -> String:
  match s:
    case SNil{}: acc
    case SCon{c, rest}: reverseOnto(rest, SCon{c, acc})

def reverseTwice(s: String) -> String:
  reverseOnto(reverseOnto(s, SNil{}), SNil{})
```

```sh
bend fuse.bend -o fuse.mjs
bun -e 'import m from "./fuse.mjs"; const s = "\udc00\ud800";
  const r = m.reverseTwice(s);
  console.log([...s].length, [...r].length, r === s)'
```

### What happened

`reverseTwice` returns `"𐀀"` (one character, U+10000) for the
input `"\udc00\ud800"` (two characters, lone surrogates): the output prints
`2 1 false`. In Bend's model `reverseTwice(s) == s` for every string.

The JS lane represents a `String` as a host string: `SCon{h, t}` is
`h + t`, and a match reads the first code point, two code units when it is
above 0xFFFF (`OPTIMIZED.String.SCon` in `bend2/comp.ts`). A lone U+D800
put in front of a string that starts with a lone U+DC00 therefore becomes a
surrogate pair, and the next match reads one character where two were
stored. A program run by `bend` cannot build these characters
(`Char.from_u32` traps, #1080), but an export receives them: JavaScript
strings may hold lone surrogates, and the export passes them as `String`
arguments or as `Char` fields of data.

Consequence in practice: a function that collects characters into a
`String` and reads it again (an accumulator reversed at the end) changes
its input; composed with a strict encoder, a text rejected for its lone
surrogates becomes the four bytes of U+10000.

### What I expected

The same characters back, as in Bend's model; or, if the JS lane
does not support characters outside the scalar range, a rejection at the
export boundary (as `char_new` does for `Char.from_u32`), so that the
model's equations hold for every value a JS function can receive.

### Suggested fix

Decide, with #1080, what a `Char` outside the scalar range means on the JS
lane, and apply it at the export boundary: reject lone surrogates in
`String` and `Char` arguments, or represent such a character so that
concatenation cannot pair it.

Thanks for this, and for the careful measurements. Removing the closure cost of a known callback is worth doing, and the 2–5× on the particle update shows it. We're closing this PR, though, because we'd rather get there another way.

**Why not this approach**

The PR inlines the callee's body at the call site with the lambda substituted. That only works for callees that don't call themselves, so a callback passed through a loop or traversal gets nothing. It's also hard to keep correct in the compiler: it needs a fuel budget, a cache that survives ANF rebuilds, and a list of exclusions. A review reproduced three crashes where the interpreter and main both give the right answer:

- **An unused or type-level lambda argument:** `ignore(x, y => ...)` or `dapply(y => U32, x)` hits `tele_unbind` on a null type in the new `emit_unfold` branch.
- **A callback right before a parameter opened as a tuple:** `bake`'s field positions overlap the callback's, so the body becomes `callback(callback, b)`.
- **Two `@unsafe` defs that tail-call each other passing the callback:** they inline into each other until the compiler's stack overflows, because the cache hit costs no fuel.

It's also C-only, and the first commit now conflicts with #1281.

**The direction we'd like instead**

Bend already specializes known callbacks with templates. `List.map`, `filter`, `any`, `all`, `find`, `sort` and `Array.map` in Base take the callback as a `~` parameter, and each call mints an instance. That covers recursive callees and both the C and JS lanes, and the checker checks the instance like any other def. The missing piece is captures:

```python
List.map(~U32, ~U32, ~(y => U32.add(y, bias)), xs)
# today: "a template applied to closed ~ arguments (bias is a variable here, not comptime: pass it at run time)"
```

The plan is to allow this: when an instance is minted, each variable the callback captures becomes an extra runtime parameter of the instance, which recursive calls pass along. Your `apply(x, callback)` would then declare `~callback`, and `run` would compile to a direct call with `bias` passed in, with no closure. We're prototyping it now and will link it here. Your fixtures (`known_callback`, `known_callback_array`) are the first tests we're running against it, and the particle example would be a great benchmark for it.

Closing: on reflection this isn't worth its cost. It changes no behavior (the assembly is identical), the claim-word layout was already readable where it's used, and the guard protects constants that can't change without revisiting the pool anyway. Not worth 233 tokens of comp.ts's cap.

Compiling the resulting C code into WASM using Emscripten is straightforward, but this does not solve the multithreading issue. The code inside a WASM module is single-threaded, just like JavaScript. Spawning a new thread involves JavaScript launching a second instance of the WASM module. While this offers certain advantages over JS workers (such as shared memory and atomics), implementing it correctly is quite complex and requires compliance with the virtual machine's security requirements.

For setting you’ve outlined, implementing part of the code by WebGPU rather than WebAssembly seems far more sensible. Whether Bend can be made to generate something like JS+WebGPU is a separate question.

Thanks, the diagnosis is right, and the change to open a family's body is needed. I pushed one commit on top (d3141f97) that turns it into a more general fix of the same root cause.

## The root cause is wider than pairs

`ty_holds` hands every argument of a datatype to its predicate as if it were a type. A pair's family is one argument that isn't a type, but there are others:
- **value indices**, as in `type Box<-n: Nat>`, where `Box<3n>` has the argument `3n`;
- **the `DUMMY` a dependent family opens with:** in `Exists(Nat, n => Box<n>)`, opening the family gives `Box<DUMMY>`;
- **quantities.**

`ty_clo` takes any of these that isn't `Typ`/`Qua`/`Min`/`Eql` for a possible closure, so with this PR alone a bang over them still puts every closure on the device. Device segments, measured as in the PR description, with a `main` that has a few host-only continuations:

| bang parameter | main | c996bfd8 | d3141f97 |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Array<U32> & Array<U32>` | 19 of 20 | 5 | 5 |
| `a: Array<U32>, b: Array<U32>` (baseline) | 5 of 20 | 5 | 5 |
| `Box<3n>` | 19 of 20 | **19** | 5 |
| `Exists(Nat, n => Box<n>)` | 19 of 20 | **19** | 5 |
| `U32 & Box<3n>` | 19 of 20 | **19** | 5 |
| `U32 & (U32 -> U32)` (a real closure) | 20 of 21 | 20 | 20 |

## The fix

`ty_holds` now walks an argument unless its parameter surely takes a value. It reads the parameter's kind from the datatype's telescope (`tld.T`), and `ty_value` says yes only when that kind is surely not a sort. That means a quantity (`Qnt`, `Min`), a datatype (its values are never types), an equality, or a function into one of those.

The polarity is deliberately conservative. Any kind it can't resolve, such as a variable, a stuck family or a def that doesn't reduce, is still walked. A missed closure fails on the device ("a function the device does not hold"), while an extra one only costs device code, which is the cost this PR removes. Sigma's second half has kind `A -> Kind(b)`, a family into a sort, so it is still walked, and your `Lam` opening still walks its body.

The same rule applies to `ty_holds`'s other two users, `js_marshal`'s Nat walk and `lay_of`'s re-entry check. Their predicates already answered `false` for values, so nothing changes for them.

## Test

`compile/gpu_reach_closure_indexed` follows `gpu_reach_closure_pair`, but goes through the paths the new rule touches. The bang takes `U32 & Exists(Nat, n => Fn<n>)`, where `Fn<-n: Nat>` holds a `U32 -> U32`. The inner pair is a datatype the walk has already seen, so only its arguments are walked: the quantities and the index are skipped as values, and the family naming `Fn` is opened.

- **With the fix:** it prints `43n` on the GPU (`--gpu on`), on the CPU (`--gpu off`), in JS and in the interpreter.
- **With a walk that skips every argument:** `--gpu on` fails with `bend: a function the device does not hold`.
- **With a walk that also skips families:** the same failure.

The device overreach itself doesn't show up in any program's output, so the table above is measured rather than pinned by a test.

Main's perf misses are cluster noise: this PR emits byte-identical C for all 17 runtime benches, so it only costs compile time.

Two things to change:

1. **The field types skip the memo on datatypes without parameters.** For such a datatype `adt.x` is `[]`, which is truthy, so `ctr_tail` runs the unmemoized `Bend.tele_fill` + `Bend.tele_unbind` for every constructor node it emits: every Succ in a Nat, every Bool in a WCon chain, every node of a user datatype without parameters. Passing `adt.x.length ? adt.x : undefined` to `ctr_doms` keeps those on the memoized path, and should win back part of the compile-time cost the description reports.

2. **Nothing tests the second commit.** `tests/reg/u32_literal_word_field` also passes with only f33d4f8d, so the changes to the word branch and the Array branch have no coverage. Its commit message says the new shapes "die on main and pass here", but they only exercise the first commit.

Three things before merging:

1. One closure that reaches a host op sends every bang that takes a closure to the CPU. `clo_host` is computed over the whole program, so a bang that takes a closure loses its bang bit even if its own closures never touch F32.show:

```python
import Base

def ap(f: F32 -> String, x: F32) -> String:
  f(x)

def ap2(f: U32 -> U32, x: U32) -> U32:
  f(x)

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  IO.print(String.append(U32.show(ap2!(y => (y + 1 : U32), 3)), String.append(" ",
    ap(y => F32.show(y), 2.5))))
```

This is `BANGS 1` on main and `BANGS 0` here, even though `ap` isn't a bang. It also happens when `ap2!` sits in a `do IO<Unit>:` block that later prints an `F32.show`, because the IO continuation is a closure. Printing a float in an IO block is common, so map-style bangs would silently drop to the CPU. Could the rule look only at closures that can reach that bang's closure parameter, or at least leave out IO continuations?

Related: `clo_host` scans `FL.clos` before the live filter, so a closure in a segment main never reaches (a def inlined into its caller still gets one) also counts. `[...FL.clos].some((c) => live.has(c) && host.has(c))` fixes that part.

2. `BANGS` still counts a direct `F32.show!` or `F32.read!`, along with other banged intrinsics. `IO.print(F32.show!(1.5))` emits `BANGS 1` with nothing for the device to run. The GPU is then probed and loaded for nothing, and `--gpu on` fails on a machine without one. Filtering `bangs` with `intr_of(k) === undefined` makes `BANGS` count only bangs that go to the device, which is what the description says.

3. The test can't fail on (1). It checks only the printed line, so it still passes if every bang goes to the host. The header says `sq` still goes to the device, but nothing checks that. Could it also check the emitted C, for example that `BANGS` is 1 or that `sq` keeps its `FID_T` bang bit, so it fails if this regresses?

Smaller, optional:
- The `host` back-closure repeats the reverse walk `forky` does a few lines below, but handles Clo~apply differently (forky adds the edge, host has the separate `wides`/`clo_host` rule). One shared helper would keep them from drifting.
- `wide`, `wides` and `clo_host` are hard to tell apart. The comment above `compile_book` could also say that one host closure moves every wide bang to the host.
- A wider alternative: if the device handed a task back to the host when it hits `ERR_FIDS`, it would cover any future op the device can't run without this analysis.

Thanks @vicmcorrea, the diagnosis is right and the fix works. I reproduced it with Apple clang 21 by adding
  -fno-common, which is upstream clang's default. On main, hello is 582 KB and your size test prints False.
  With the PR it's 70 KB and prints True. The duplicate-registration and alien-request errors are unchanged.
  All gates pass, and the emitted C differs only in the table and dispatch lines.

  Also worth knowing: Apple clang leaves the table as a common symbol, and that's why dropping `static` in
  #1281 looked like a fix. Our gate machines use Apple clang, so the new size test passes on main there and
  can't catch a revert. It only catches one on Linux or Homebrew clang.

  One ask: instead of `volatile`, could the table be sized to the program's constructor ids?

      Effect io_eff_rows[sizeof CID_T / sizeof *CID_T];

  Every CID(k) an effect registers, and every request io_step dispatches, is already a row of CID_T (cid_arity
  reads it first). The table then has a few dozen rows (117 at most in the test corpus), so it doesn't matter
  whether clang folds it. That holds with -fno-common, -flto and gcc, and needs no volatile access or change to
  io_step. With it, hello is 54 KB with -fno-common and 53 KB with -flto. It's +18 tokens on comp.ts, against
  +12 for the PR. Your two tests can stay as they are.

Thanks @MuhDur, the diagnosis is right: safe.ts picks one model per ~ constant at a time, and that is why v_n
  never reached the kernel. But this PR doesn't fix #1182, so we're closing it.

  Why it doesn't fix #1182: I rebased it onto current main and ran leo-guinan's three repros (
  higher_evidence_base, law_higher_evidence_probe, dependent_empty_result_probe). All three still fail
  --verdict with no model for use~F, both on this branch and on main. Their ~F is an injectivity proof ({S{a}
  == S{b}} -> {a == b}). The model search builds models from constructors and constants only, so it can't
  produce one, and searching harder doesn't help. Backtracking only helps when a root has several ~ constants
  that each have a model but the first ones picked don't fit together. That's your v_n and bend-mathlib's
  algebra and order, not the issue as reported.

  Why we'd rather not take it as a partial fix:

  • It adds about 900 ttok to safe.ts. Fixing the problems below brings that to about 1,400, which leaves 336

Repro file (this is `tests/io/chan_try_late.bend` verbatim from 2.0.36 / commit 1d895ca — the race is between the effect loop and wall-clock timers, so it does not minimize below this program):

```python
# io (io_chan_try_late): a try_ deadline that passes in the same loop pass
# as an earlier timer still withdraws its waiter before anything runs, on
# every lane. A receive bounded by 10 ms parks, a sender sleeps 1 ms, and a
# busy computation holds the loop past both. The sender's timer is due
# first, but the receive's deadline has passed too: it answers Wait{}, the
# sender finds no receiver and parks, and the recv after the Wait takes
# its 7.
import Base

def spin(n: Nat, acc: U32) -> U32:
  match n:
    case 0n:
      acc
    case 1n+p:
      spin(p, (acc * 1664525 + 1013904223 : U32))

def show(r: Poll<&1, &1, Maybe<&1, U32>, Unit>) -> String:
  match r:
    case Ready{Some{v}}:
      "A: ready got " ++ U32.show(v)
    case Ready{None{}}:
      "A: ready ended"
    case Wait{u}:
      "A: wait"

def got(m: Maybe<&1, U32>) -> String:
  match m:
    case Some{v}:
      "A: then got " ++ U32.show(v)
    case None{}:
      "A: then ended"

def send(+c: Chan(U32)) -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    Unit <- IO.sleep(1)
    Result<&1, &1, U32, Unit> <- Chan.send(U32, c, 7)
    IO.print("S: sent")

def spun(m: Maybe<&1, Nat>) -> IO(Unit):
  match m:
    case Some{n}:
      IO.print("B: " ++ U32.show(spin(n, 0)))
    case None{}:
      IO.print("B: none")

# The count crosses a channel, so no build folds the spin.
def busy(+d: Chan(Nat)) -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    Result<&1, &1, Nat, Unit> <- Chan.send(Nat, d, 50000000n)
    m : Maybe<&1, Nat> <- Chan.recv(Nat, d)
    spun(m)

def recv(+c: Chan(U32), d: Chan(Nat)) -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    Unit <- IO.spawn(Unit, send(c))
    Unit <- IO.spawn(Unit, busy(d))
    r : Poll<&1, &1, Maybe<&1, U32>, Unit> <- Chan.try_recv(U32, c, 10)
    Unit <- IO.print(show(r))
    m : Maybe<&1, U32> <- Chan.recv(U32, c)
    IO.print(got(m))

def go(c: Chan(U32)) -> IO(Unit):
  IO.bind(Chan(Nat), Unit, Chan.new(Nat, 1), d => recv(c, d))

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  IO.bind(Chan(U32), Unit, Chan.new(U32, 0), go)

#|B: 767263360
#|A: wait
#|A: then got 7
#|S: sent
```

Thank you for this, @aivv73! It's a careful, well-tested piece of work: the ownership handling, the `XSync` detail and the external-process checks all show real thought.

We've decided not to take it into Base, though. Base tries to keep only what every backend can offer, and `WindowRef` would be a public type whose only constructor is X11-specific, returning `ENOTSUP` on macOS, JS and Wayland sessions. Once it's in, each new backend would have to follow it (Wayland handles, `NSWindow`, HWND…), and that's a direction we'd like to keep Base out of.

This would make a great BendHub package instead, and it should work today. A package can ship its own foreign `.c`/`.js` effect, and `bend --publish` sends them with it. The effect's C lands in the same translation unit as Base's `window.c`, after it, so your effect body can stay almost exactly as it is in this PR:

```python
def WinRef.export(window: Window) ->
  IO(Window & Result<&1, &1, U32 & String, WindowRef>):
  import "./winref.c"
  import "./winref.js"
```

with `window_export_ref_run` moved into `winref.c` (casting `io_hand_v(f[0])` to `BendWin*`) and registered under `CID(WinRef.export)`. One caveat: `BendWin` is a runtime internal, not a stable interface, so the package may need a touch-up if the runtime's window struct changes.

If you publish it, we'd be happy to hear about it, and if a concrete use case later shows Base needs a backend-neutral way to hand out native handles, an issue about that would be very welcome. Thanks again for the contribution!
Closing along with #1241: we'd rather not add an X11-specific type to Base, but this fits well as a BendHub package. See #1241 for details. Thanks for the clear proposal, @aivv73!

The same fault reproduces on the **CUDA lane**, at the same boundary — this doesn't look Metal-specific after all. Measured on Linux x86_64, bend 2.0.36 (commit 1d895ca), NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (driver 595.91.07, CUDA 13.2), bun 1.4.2, clang 21.

### What you did

Non-tail recursion under a bang, with the list built tail-recursively so construction is not the source of depth (the recursion being tested is the sum walk):

```python
import Base

def lsum(xs: List<&1, U32>) -> U32:
  match xs:
    case Nil{}:
      0
    case Con{h, t}:
      (h + lsum(t) : U32)

def build(n: Nat, acc: List<&1, U32>) -> List<&1, U32>:
  match n:
    case 0n:
      acc
    case 1n+p:
      build(p, Con{1, acc})

def probe(n: Nat) -> U32:
  lsum(build(n, Nil{}))

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    c : U32 = probe!(2000n)
    IO.print(U32.show(c))
```

### What happened

By depth, on the same binary:

| list length | `./t --gpu off` (CPU pool) | `./t` (CUDA) |
|---|---|---|
| 1000 / 1022 | correct | correct |
| **1023** | correct | `bend: memory fault (machine stack overflow?)` |
| 1024 … 1,000,000 | correct | `bend: memory fault (machine stack overflow?)` |

The 1023/1024 boundary matches this issue's Metal threshold exactly, 10/10 deterministic at n=2000 — so the per-lane device stack cap looks shared by (or mirrored in) the CUDA build, not a Metal quirk. The CPU pool completes through 1,000,000 elements, as here.

For completeness, two adjacent CUDA-path behaviors checked while there (both *clean*, both negative results for their respective open issues): with `--gpu 512MB`/`--gpu 1GB` caps, exceeding the device heap reports the graceful `bend: out of memory: run again with a bigger span, as in --gpu 8GB` and exits 1 (#1300's fault/hang class did not reproduce on CUDA at the allocation-failure points I could construct); and a large `[0 : U32^28n]` allocation inside a bang does run on the device (visible in nvidia-smi) but takes ~20 s of *host* CPU time where `--gpu off` does the same work in 1.2 s wall — possibly the same per-lane serialization, possibly host-side page servicing; I did not chase that down far enough to call it a finding.

Thanks again, @oxura! Before merging I cut this down to the core fix, which is now one line in `safe.ts` plus your two tests:

```diff
-      if (x.k === "Nat" && x.v > NAT_MAX) {
+      if (x.k === "Nat" && x.v > NAT_MAX && e.book.tlds.Nat?.b === true) {
```

Why:

- **One guard covers it.** `Nat.mul` and `Nat.add` are the only names `safe.ts` inserts by itself. If `Nat` is Base's, Base is imported, and then those two can't be redefined (a duplicate declaration is an error). So checking `Nat` alone is enough, the same way `comp.ts` trusts the Base names it relies on.
- **`nat_literal` wasn't needed.** Without the compact form, a user Nat literal takes the same path as every other literal (`lit_step`, then `ctr_term`), which builds the same constructor chain. Across the 597 tests with literals, the kernel output is byte-for-byte identical with and without `nat_literal`.
- **It didn't prevent the stack overflow either.** A later `safe.ts` pass recurses once per layer over the finished term anyway. With plain recursion, `nat_literal`, or a general loop-built lowering, a user Nat literal of about 10,000 overflows at the same size. Around that size the checker overflows first anyway. So keeping it added a second way to build literals without making anything work that didn't before.

Very large literals of a user-defined Nat (and very long strings) still overflow the stack. That's a separate issue: some recursions in the checker and in `safe.ts` go one level per layer. It also crashes rather than accepting anything wrong, so it isn't unsound.

Checked: both new tests and `9000n` under Base pass `--verdict`, and `gates/_run.ts` gives repo 50/50 and test 1578/1578.

**Update on 2.0.36** (commit 1d895ca, Linux x86_64, bun 1.4.2), re-verified in isolation — and a wider set of entry points that hit the same JS-side abort:

- The **interpreter half of this issue has been fixed**: `Char.from_u32(55296)` now checks, runs and prints `"\u{d800}"` on lane 0 (`bend t.bend`). The C lane prints it too. Only the **JS lane still aborts**: `bend: 55296 is not a Unicode scalar value`, exit 1, through `chr_new`'s scalar check.
- The abort is broader than `Char.from_u32`, and reaches string **literals**:

```python
import Base

def main() -> String:
  "a\u{d800}b"
```

  - interpreter: `"a\u{d800}b"` (exit 0); C: same (exit 0);
    `bend t.bend -o t.js && bun t.js`: `bend: 55296 is not a Unicode scalar value`, exit 1.
  - the same file with `u{110000}` or `u{ffffffff}`: interpreter/C print `'\u{110000}'` / `'\u{ffffffff}'`; JS aborts with the same message. `Char.from_u32(1114112)` and `Char.from_u32(4294967295)` likewise.
  - it fires even when the bad code is never shown — `String.length`/`String.eq`/`String.is_empty` over such a value abort the JS program the moment the value crosses `chr_new`.
- Front-end intent (for whoever fixes it): `lit_of` (bend.ts ~1077-1083) deliberately keeps a literal spelling a surrogate or a codepoint past U+10FFFF as an explicit `SCon` chain, and `chr_show` (~1288-1297) deliberately renders it — so the abort contradicts both the checker's own representable-literal model and the C lane, rather than guarding an invariant the language has.
- C-side note, same family: through `IO.print` the C backend writes a lone surrogate as raw invalid UTF-8 (`ed a0 80`) since `io_utf8` (comp.ts ~5502) does not clamp — the C lane is fine on the pure/show path, only the byte-output side is unclamped.

**Correction to my earlier comment above** — the interpreter half of this is only fixed for *pure* evaluation, not for the IO-run machinery every real program uses (2.0.36, commit 1d895ca, re-verified in isolation):

```python
import Base

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    IO.print(U32.show(Char.to_u32(Char.from_u32(4294967295))))
    IO.print(U32.show(Char.to_u32(Char.from_u32(65536))))
    IO.print(U32.show(Char.to_u32(Char.from_u32(55296))))
```

- interpreter (`bend t.bend`): `bend: 4294967295 is not a Unicode scalar value`, exit 1;
- the same computation with a pure `main -> U32` / `main -> String` normalizes and prints correctly (`4294967295`, `5`, …), so the plain-value path was indeed fixed;
- JS lane: throws in every shape (pure and IO);
- C lane: accepts the full U32 range everywhere.

So the current three-lane state is: C fine everywhere; interpreter fine for pure programs, throwing under the IO run; JS throwing everywhere. Bonus oddity found while minimizing: inside one interpreter IO-run, the *generic* route building a `List<&2, Char>` of such chars folded by specialized readers succeeds with the correct value, while the direct `Char.from_u32` beside it throws (`61-char-code-range-divergence-generic.bend` in the linked campaign directory) — the check is per-routing rather than per-language.

**Single-row extremity** of the same mechanism, worth knowing when sizing the fix (2.0.36, commit 1d895ca, re-verified in isolation): it doesn't take thousands of rows. **One** match row spelling the numeral the guide explicitly documents as the supported maximum —

```python
import Base

def main(x : Nat) -> Nat:
  match x:
    case 4294967295n:
      1n
    case other:
      0n
```

— makes the checker die at load on every lane with the formatted overflow (`SOME PROOFS FAIL / Error: the machine stack overflowed (a deep recursion, or a literal too large to expand)`, exit 1). The guide documents Nat literals up to `4294967295n` as `U32.to_nat(n)` underneath, so this row is legal surface, not a pathological file: it is precisely the "literal too large to expand" case the error message names.

Determined thresholds on this machine (bun 1.4.2, stack knob unset): rows of 5000n and 6000n check and run; a single 100000n row dies; 4294967295n dies deterministically (2/2). Another campaign pass measured the single-row boundary at ~6000n with `BUN_JSC_maxPerThreadStackUsage=33554432` — either way the documented maximum is far past it, and unlike the multi-row quadratic cost above, the single-row case means a whole *class* of legal programs (any `match` on a Nat with a near-max literal case) cannot be checked at all, on any lane.

Found by the same automated AI-model campaign as the parent issue (numeric deep pass, ~4,400 oracle-checked lines); reproductions re-verified in isolation before posting.

One more witness for the same class, from the string-parsing direction (2.0.36, re-verified): `F32.read("-nan")` diverges the same way — the C lane parses it with `strtof` and yields bits `0xFFC00000` (negative quiet NaN), while the interpreter and JS lanes answer the canonical positive `0x7FC00000`, so even `F32.bits(F32.read("-nan"))` is lane-unstable before any Constructor surgery. Everything *around* the NaN range checked bit-exact in this pass: 552 adversarial `F32.read` strings (exact f32-midpoint decimals, `2^128−2^103` overflow tie, `"1."`, `".5e1"`, hex rejection, whitespace forms) agreed bit-for-bit between JS and C, as did ~1000 transcendental/op evaluations, subnormals, −0.0 comparisons and conversions at 0xFFFFFFFF — the canonicalization is confined to NaN-class values exactly as the bit-flip repro suggests.

Thanks for this, and for the thorough benchmarks. The speedup is real. But I don't think this belongs in Base, so I'm closing it. It would work as a library instead.

**It isn't shaped like any Base effect.** Base's effects are thin syscall wrappers. Their arguments and results are only `U32`, `String`, `List`, handles and `Result`s, and none of them takes or returns an `Array`. `File.read_into` would be the first that writes into a Bend value's memory: the IO helper thread `pread`s straight into the heap through `blk_loc`. It would also make its rules part of Base's contract: the partial last slot keeps its high bytes, and a forked handle sees the writes.

**A library can do exactly the same thing.** `guide/EFFECTS.md`: a user effect's `.c` is spliced in after the runtime with every runtime symbol in scope, and its `.js` registers the same way Base's do. So the same def works from any module:

```
def File.read_into(file: File, offset: U32, max: U32, a: Array<U32>, at: U32) ->
  IO(File & (Array<U32> & Result<&1, &1, U32 & String, U32>)):
  import "./file_read_into.c"
  import "./file_read_into.js"
```

Your C and JS bodies move over almost unchanged. `tests/io/cid_capture_lib.bend` is an example of this pattern. The model loader can ship it next to its own code.

The trade-off is that the C side reaches undocumented internals (`blk_loc`, `blk_cls`, `e.mem`), and EFFECTS.md makes no ABI promise, so the library has to track runtime renames. That's the same deal every custom effect has.

If the underlying issue is that `File.read_at`'s one-`List`-node-per-byte result is too slow for binary data, a Base-shaped fix would be a general byte primitive rather than an effect that fills one array type. If you want to pursue that, please open an issue first.

Thanks for picking this up. #1470 fixes the same issue, and this PR has two gaps that it closes:

1. **No regression test.** The description says a `#|` expectation can't express a broken pipe, but it can: the test only needs a child whose stdout or stderr is a pipe with its read end already closed. #1470 adds `tests/io/stream_epipe.bend` with `.c` and `.js` twins. The C twin forks a child that writes through `io_out`/`io_sync`. The JS twin spawns a child `bun` that runs the runtime's own `io_out`. Each prints the child's status: `141` for fd 1 and fd 2 on all three lanes (checkup, C, JS). On main it prints the message and `1`. Closing the read end before the write keeps it deterministic.

2. **The JS lane doesn't end by SIGPIPE.** `process.exit(141)` is a normal exit with status 141, so the two lanes disagree for any parent that checks how a child ended. `waitpid` reports `WIFSIGNALED` for the C binary and `WIFEXITED` for `bun x.js`; Python's `subprocess`, for example, reports `-13` for one and `141` for the other. Bun ignores SIGPIPE, but adding and then removing a listener restores `SIG_DFL` (`onDidChangeListeners` in Bun's `BunProcess.cpp`, the same in 1.2 and 1.4). #1470's `io_out` does that and signals itself, so both lanes end the same way.

Smaller points: `io_out` only ever receives `stdout`/`stderr` (fd 1/2 in JS; `file_write.js` has its own loop), so the `h == stdout || h == stderr` and `fd === 1 || fd === 2` checks are always true. The braceless one-line `if` also differs from the surrounding style.

#1470 covers the C lane, the JS lane and the in-process `bend f.bend` run, adds the test, and stays under comp.ts's cap (63,997 ttok), so I'd suggest closing this one in its favor.

Same limit on CUDA here, but whether you hit it depends on how many tasks the bang spreads to. While some lanes are free, a lane can recurse much deeper than 1,023. Once every lane has a task, any recursion past about 1,024 calls faults. Measured on main (d5fe6566), RTX 3090, driver 615.71, CUDA 13.1.

This forks 2^d leaves under one bang. Leaf i builds a list of n copies of i and sums it with the same non-tail `lsum` as above:

```python
import Base

type T is Type:
  Leaf{x: U32}
  Node{l: T, r: T}

def lsum(xs: List<&1, U32>) -> U32:
  match xs:
    case Nil{}:
      0
    case Con{h, t}:
      (h + lsum(t) : U32)

def build(n: Nat, +v: U32, acc: List<&1, U32>) -> List<&1, U32>:
  match n:
    case 0n:
      acc
    case 1n+p:
      build(p, v, Con{v, acc})

def leaves(+d: Nat, +i: U32, +n: Nat) -> T:
  match d:
    case 0n:
      Leaf{lsum(build(n, i, Nil{}))}
    case 1n+e:
      x y = leaves(e, U32.mul(i, 2), n) leaves(e, U32.add(U32.mul(i, 2), 1), n)
      Node{x, y}

def total(t: T) -> U32:
  match t:
    case Leaf{x}:
      x
    case Node{l, r}:
      U32.add(total(l), total(r))

def go(md: Maybe<&2, Nat>, mn: Maybe<&2, Nat>) -> IO(Unit):
  match md mn:
    case Some{+d} Some{+n}:
      IO.print(U32.show(total(leaves!(d, 0, n))))
    case _ _:
      IO.print("usage: deep log2_leaves n")

def dispatch(args: List<String>) -> IO(Unit):
  match args:
    case Con{p, Con{d, Con{n, Nil{}}}}:
      go(Nat.read(d), Nat.read(n))
    case _:
      IO.print("usage: deep log2_leaves n")

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    args : List<String> <- IO.args()
    dispatch(args)
```

`./deep D N --gpu 8GB`, each list N long:

| Leaves under the bang | N = 1,000 | N = 1,100 | N = 20,000 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | ok | ok | ok |
| 4,096 | ok | ok | ok |
| 8,192 | ok | memory fault | memory fault |
| 16,384 | ok | memory fault | memory fault |

`--gpu off` gets every cell right, and a 20 GB heap faults the same way. The 3090 has 82 SMs, so `CUBE_LOG` is 6 and the bag is 128 << 6 = 8,192 lanes ([comp.ts#L5019](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/d5fe65662e02cce0261ad58234c2466f39a0736d/bend2/comp.ts#L5019)): the fault starts exactly when there are as many leaves as lanes. The single-leaf row is interesting too: the same `lsum` 20,000 deep works as one leaf of `leaves!`, but `probe!(2000n)` from the comment above still faults on this commit. So I'd guess the fork-free case, or the case where every lane is busy, runs on the fixed lane stack (`STAK_LEN` 2^11 words, [comp.ts#L3501](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/d5fe65662e02cce0261ad58234c2466f39a0736d/bend2/comp.ts#L3501)), and `WL_ROOM` posts `ERR_DEEP` when it fills ([comp.ts#L3423](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/d5fe65662e02cce0261ad58234c2466f39a0736d/bend2/comp.ts#L3423)). I haven't confirmed that though.

This is what caps the batch size in a real workload. I run nanoGPT inference as a batch of independent generations, one per leaf, over shared weights ([bend-bench ML.md](https://github.com/wakamex/bend-bench/blob/main/ML.md)). It works up to 4,096 sequences and faults within a second from 8,192, at any heap size, while the CPU runs 8,192 fine. So the GPU never gets past half its lanes on that workload.

Two smaller things:
- The message for `ERR_DEEP`, "memory fault (machine stack overflow?)", sounds like a heap or host problem. Something like "a GPU lane's stack is full: recursion deeper than about 1,000 calls" would have saved me a few rounds of heap sizes.
- The same limit hits joins, not just leaves. My first batch appended each half's list of results at every join, and that recursion overflowed at 2,048 sequences. Returning a tree instead fixed it.

Thanks @totaland, and good to hear you're building an inference engine on Bend.

On moving the kernels: Base and the compiler are only for really basic things, the primitives every Bend program needs. Inference kernels (rmsnorm, quantized matmul, attention and so on) are too specific for that.

The right place for them is your own package. If you need hand-written C there, a foreign effect can import it (`def e(x: A) -> IO(B):` with `import "./e.c"`, see the GUIDE), and that C can drive Metal or CUDA itself. It runs from the event loop on the host, not inside `!`, but for an inference engine that is usually how kernels get launched anyway.

About the 1.6%: if you share a repro (the program, the machine and before/after numbers over several runs), we're happy to look at why the package version is slower. If it comes from something general in the compiler, we'd rather fix that for everyone than move model-specific code into it.

Another shape of the same mismatch, still present on **2.0.36**. Here the `~` function has a model only together with the other `~` constant: it is the step hypothesis of a generic invariant `~P`.

```bend
import Base

def lift(~P: @+n: Nat -> Bool, ~H: @+n: Nat -> @_: {P(n) == True{} : Bool} -> {P(1n+n) == True{} : Bool}, +n: Nat, h: {P(n) == True{} : Bool}) -> {P(1n+n) == True{} : Bool}:
  H(n, h)

def twice(~P: @+n: Nat -> Bool, ~H: @+n: Nat -> @_: {P(n) == True{} : Bool} -> {P(1n+n) == True{} : Bool}, +n: Nat, h: {P(n) == True{} : Bool}) -> {P(2n+n) == True{} : Bool}:
  H(1n+n, H(n, h))
```

```
$ bend h.bend --check-only
ALL PROOFS CHECK
$ bend h.bend --verdict
SOME PROOFS FAIL
Sorry - this is a mismatch between the TypeScript implementation, and the formalized BendTT kernel. ...
$ bend h.bend -o h.bendtt
BendTT: out of scope, so not in h.bendtt:
- lift: no model for lift~H
- twice: no model for lift~H
```

What I found while narrowing it down:

- `~P` with no `~H` passes `--verdict`.
- Making `H` an ordinary parameter (`H:`) also passes `--verdict` for `lift`. It cannot fix `twice`, because `twice` uses `H` twice: an ordinary function parameter is linear, and `+` on a function type is refused (`expected : Data / observed : Type`). So once a proof uses its hypothesis in more than one place, a `~` parameter is the only way to write it.
- A model does exist (`P := λn. True{}`, `H := λn. λh. h`), so this is the "constants that must fit together" case that #1263 addressed, not the injectivity case in the original report. Using checked defs as models, the direction suggested when #1263 was closed, would not cover it: `H` is an abstract hypothesis, and no closed def of its type exists in the book.
- `twice`'s entry names `lift~H`, not `twice~H`. That may be a separate labelling slip in the out-of-scope report.

Impact: this is the usual shape of a preservation proof. You state an invariant once as `~P`, take one `~H` per operation saying the operation keeps `P`, and then induct over a run, applying each `H` once per step. In a scheduler core I am verifying, about 30 such lemmas sit under two top-level laws. Both pass `--check-only` and fail `--verdict` only because of this. The workaround is to instantiate every lemma for each concrete invariant, which multiplies the proof by the number of invariants.

Still reproduces on 2.0.36 (also 2.0.34 and 2.0.35). A smaller reproducer, and what `-o` says about it:

```bend
import Base

def k(~P: Nat, ~f: Nat -> {P == 1n : Nat}, x: Nat) -> {P == 1n : Nat}:
  f(x)
```

```text
$ bend t1.bend --check-only
ALL PROOFS CHECK
$ bend t1.bend --verdict
SOME PROOFS FAIL
Sorry - this is a mismatch between the TypeScript implementation, and the formalized BendTT kernel. ...
$ bend t1.bend -o t1.bendtt
BendTT: out of scope, so not in t1.bendtt:
- k: no model for k~f
```

The `.bendtt` file gives `~P` the model `opaque k_7e_P : Nat = (.Zero, ())`. With that model, the type of `~f`, `Nat -> {0 == 1 : Nat}`, has no inhabitant, so the translation has no model for `~f` and leaves `k` out. Changing only the literal agrees with that reading:

| result type of `~f` | `--verdict` |
|---|---|
| `{P == 0n : Nat}` | ALL PROOFS CHECK |
| `{P == 1n : Nat}` | SOME PROOFS FAIL |
| `{1n == P : Nat}` | SOME PROOFS FAIL |
| `{P == P : Nat}` | ALL PROOFS CHECK |
| `{1n == 1n : Nat}` (no `~P`) | ALL PROOFS CHECK |
| `{P == 1n : Nat}`, `f` not a template | ALL PROOFS CHECK |
| `{P == 1n : Nat}`, `~f` never applied | ALL PROOFS CHECK |

The Bool version, `~P: Bool` with `~f: Nat -> {P == True{} : Bool}`, fails the same way.

Thanks for the report. We closed #1474 because we don't want main's return value to become the exit status, since that changes the meaning of every existing `IO(U32)` main.

The direction we'd take instead:

1. Add `IO.exit(code: U32) -> IO(A)`, which exits with `code` and writes nothing to stderr. That covers the CLI case: print your own multi-line usage error, then `IO.exit(2)`. You no longer need a foreign `exit()`, so #1463 stops getting in the way too.
2. Have `IO.die` and `IO.exit` check that the code is in 0..255. Today an out-of-range code wraps mod 256 (`IO.die(256, "x")` exits 0). It should fail with a nonzero status instead.

Thanks for the report. Neither case is unsound: in both, Bend proves a true fact about the program as it was parsed, and the kernel agrees. The surprise is in how the source was read, not in the checker.

### 1. `3n * 0n+0n + 5n`

The guide says operators need spaces on both sides (guide/GUIDE.md:635). A `+` glued to the left of a term is not the addition operator. `kn+t` is the Nat literal form "k plus t", the same one used in `case 1n+p:` patterns and in `1n+length(a, A, t)` (guide/GUIDE.md:241). It takes the rest of the expression as `t`, so the claim was read as:

```python
{(3n * 0n+(0n + 5n) : Nat) == 15n : Nat}   # 3 * (0 + (0 + 5)) = 15, which is true
```

That checks, and so does `(3n * (0n + 0n + 5n) : Nat) == 15n`. With the spacing the guide asks for, or with the parens you meant, the false claim is rejected:

```python
def Foo() -> {(3n * 0n + 0n + 5n : Nat) == 15n : Nat}:    # SOME PROOFS FAIL
def Foo() -> {((3n * 0n) + 0n + 5n : Nat) == 15n : Nat}:  # SOME PROOFS FAIL
def Foo() -> {((3n * 0n) + 0n + 5n : Nat) == 5n : Nat}:   # ALL PROOFS CHECK
```

### 2. The misaligned `case x`

A match's cases are the `case` lines indented at least as far as its first case. The inner `match b` has its cases at 8 spaces. `case x` is at 7, so it ends the inner match and becomes a case of the outer `match a`, whose cases are at 4. The function was parsed as:

```python
def p4m(a: Bool, b: Bool) -> Nat:
  match a:
    case True{}:
      match b:
        case True{}:
          1n
        case False{}:
          2n
    case x:          # catches False{}
      7n
    case False{}:    # unreachable: the first matching case wins
      3n
```

So `p4m(False{}, True{})` really is `7n`. Running it prints `7n`, and the proof is correct for this program. With `case x` aligned to the inner cases, as you intended, the function returns `3n` and the false claim is rejected:

```text
SOME PROOFS FAIL
- expected : 3n
- observed : 7n
Location: Foo
```

A proof is about the program Bend parsed. If the source is read differently from what you meant, the proof is still right about the program that runs. That is a readability problem (an unreachable case could be a warning, for example), not a false theorem. Closing as not planned for now.

On the bounty: it covers holes in the theory, i.e. Bend accepting a proof of something false (ultimately, a proof of `Empty`). These don't qualify, since every claim here is true of the program that was checked.

• Description: the guide now explains it. A package's description is the # comment on the first line of its
  first .bend file (sorted by path). For example, put # A JSON parser and printer at the top of main.bend. If
  there's no comment there, the package has no description.
• License: a name's page now shows the license of its latest version, like package pages do (a link to the
  LICENSE file, or "MIT-0 (default)" if there isn't one).

  About your other questions:

  • Yanking: there's no yank, and that's on purpose. In npm or cargo, yanking matters because the tool picks
    versions for you from a range like ^1.2. On BendHub nothing is picked for you. Every import names an exact
    name@version or hash, and a published package never changes, so there's nothing to yank. To fix a bad
    version, publish a higher one.

  • Four numbers: yes, that was a choice because of "hash bumping", but maybe we could have only 3 slots to be exactly semver. But you can use semver in the first 3 as well.

  • Open source: as I said above, BendHub isn't open source for now, but issues here are welcome. Just tag me.

  Closing this, but feel free to reopen if something still looks off.

bend lib/tensor_f32.bend --publish stelliferous@0.0.3.0

I pushed 4984a328 on top of this PR. It's a small simplification: the JS `io_wait` goes back to main's two `filter` passes. On the `EBADF` path, `due` asks `fcntl`, and a closed descriptor is still closed on the second pass, so the loop didn't need to be rewritten. This saves 13 tokens.

I also looked at moving `io_wait` to `poll()`, which reports `POLLNVAL` for each bad descriptor. That doesn't work here: comp.ts says macOS `poll` misses FIFO EOF, which is why `io_wait` uses `select`. So probing with `F_GETFD` only after an `EBADF` looks like the right approach to me.
